speakerposition: topic
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT

speakerposition: stagedirection
Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The present Opium and
Narcotic Act was passed in 1911. At our last session the law of 1911 was very substantially amended. Since then the department has had the experience of nearly a year in the administration of that law and the object of these amendments is to tighten up the law to some extent and to make more certain that those who are carrying on illicit traffic in drugs shall be convicted. If we take up the paragraphs of the resolution one by one I can make any explanation that is necessary. I understand that certain members of the committee desire to express their views with regard to some of the proposed amendments.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Paragraph 1 provides
that no prescription is to be used more than once. Have any complaints been received that the privilege of using more than once a prescription made out for a patient by a physician has been abused?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: A number of complaints have reached the department of abuses in connection with the use of prescriptions given by physicians for fairly large doses of narcotic drugs. One case was brought to my attention where a drug addict, without reference to his physician, used a prescription for a fairly large dose several times and the prescription was filled by the druggist. I understand there have been numerous cases of that kind, and the department advises, in order to put an end to those abuses, that any prescription given for this purpose should be used only once, and that if the drug is to be used further, a fresh prescription should be called for in each case.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I can hardly understand the instance which the minister points out, because a druggist is supposed to take possession of the prescription. I think the trouble is that the druggist has held the prescription and has refilled the same prescription more than once.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I dare say that is the case.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is the refilling of a prescription without an order from the physician.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is it a common thing to refill a prescription?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes, it is a common thing for prescriptions for simple cough mixtures to be refilled, but prescriptions for dangerous medicines or medicines of this kind should not be refilled.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I should
be glad, in the interest of the public, if the minister would cut out this clause. It is a hardship, especially on poor people, to have to go back to a medical man and pay a couple of dollars every time they want a prescription refilled. Within the last hour or two I have had a couple of gentlemen tell me that they have had to pay $2 to a medical man, not in the House of Commons, but in the city of Ottawa, just for the privilege of getting a fresh prescription for a particular medicine that seemed to suit the case pretty well;-I might say that the reason for getting it was no breach of the Ontario Temperance Act. It is a hardship on a number of poor people, who are taking a certain class of medicine more or less continuously, to compel them to go back to a doctor, and it is an inf-dignity on the medical profession to make them rewrite a prescription which will possibly cost the man or woman who gets it a couple of dollars. I realize the object that the minister and his department have in view, in bringing forward this legislation, namely, the curtailment of the drug habit; but, after all, we must remember this, that we are legislating here for the great mass of the people, and not for the few. While we have a few morphine and opium fiends in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and probably Calgary and Vancouver, throughout the great length and breadth of this country there is practically none. I am speaking in the interest of the ordinary man who finds it a hardship to pay a couple of dollars simply to have a prescription refilled. When he consulted his physician on the first occasion, he paid for the advice and the prescription; the prescription is his, and all that this Parliament does is to say to him: "You cannot have your property refilled without going to extra expense."

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The word "prescription" under this resolution refers 
only to prescriptions for opium, not generally compounded drugs containing opium.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If you
give a prescription for an ordinary cough mixture that contains a little heroin or codein or paregoric, that prescription cannot be refilled. There may be half a dozen other things in such a prescription, and that is the kind of prescription I am referring to. If you are going to limit the restriction to pure drugs such as opium or morphine, I have no objection; but I object to this clause on behalf of the ordinary man or woman who is using these drugs more or less in prescription form. This is an infringement on their rights and we should not pass it.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I understand the minister to say that this refers just to prescriptions containing morphine and opium, is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Opium and other narcotic drugs.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: A point which my hon. friend (Mr. McGibbon) seems to forget when he speaks of the two dollars having to be paid to doctors on all occasions, is the fact that a man might be given a prescription for morphine or opium, not necessarily from his doctor, not knowing that it contains morphine or opium. If he did not have to go back to a doctor to get a fresh prescription, an accident might occur, and there have been many occasions where the refilling of such a prescription without orders has caused the forming of a habit in the patient. I think personally that clause is a very good one just as it stands, so long as it is limited to the provision for morphine or opium or drugs which are likely to cause a habit being formed.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: All of these amendments refer only to opium and other narcotic drugs, not to the use of other drugs at all. I might further state that a similar provision to this is contained in both the British law and in the United States law known as the Harrison law.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not want to obstruct this clause, but I still desire to press my views on the committee. I object, on behalf of the ordinary man and woman, to all these irritating restrictions -for they are nothing more nor less than that. The more such restrictions we enact, the more trouble we are going to get into. Last year and the year before we passed Bills which are causing and have caused

a lot of irritation, trouble and expense to ordinary people. I fought the Bill last year in this House, and with the assistance of members of the House, we got the Bill modified to a great extent. This is just one more of those meddlesome things that this House should not pass.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Name some of the others.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I might name them later on. It is a hardship to ordinary people, for instance working men, to have to go and pay $2 every time they want a prescription refilled, that $2 being probably two or three times the cost of the medicine. This is an infringement on such a man's rights and an expense that we have no right to impose upon him. Nearly all cough medicines, for example, especially medicines for acute, irritating coughs, contain some opium or the by-products of opium, and you are going at once to wipe out the possibility of refilling any of that class of prescription without a man being compelled to go back to a medical man and pay him a dollar or two dollars simply for doing a little clerical work and signing his name. The only object in this clause is that you are endeavouring to curtail, I was going to say the establishment of drug fiends. If you cannot do this in any other way, then restrict the provision to the large cities, because there are practically no drug fiends in the country districts. In my twenty years' practice in medicine, I have met only one drug fiend, and I think my practice is a fair average in a rural district. Why are you going to penalize all the rest of the people for the sake of a few maniacs in the cities?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is it not a fact that there are many patent medicines for which you do not need to have any prescription and which contain many narcotic drugs?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Not now. That is one of the things that we practically put out of business a year ago. There are a few proprietary medicines where the prescription is printed on the bottle, which contain a certain quantity of narcotic drugs-I think, about one grain to two ounces, a very small amount.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
You can buy
those patent medicines without a prescription?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I was going to suggest that the minister will probably
expedite the final passage of his Bill if he secures the printing as early as possible and the circulating of it somewhat, so that the drug trade, and also representatives of the medical profession, may have an opportunity of making representations to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If there is no objection on the part of the Committee, perhaps it might be as well to pass the resolution on the understanding that the House is not committing itself to the principle. Then we can get the Bill printed and distributed, so that hon. members and people interested outside the House may beeome familiar with its provisions.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am very much
impressed by the argument of the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon). I can well imagine the case of a man who lives perhaps 20 or 30 miles from a doctor wanting to have his prescription refilled at a little drug store away out in the country. He is not a drug fiend and has no propensities in that direction. His child or his wife may have been ill, and the medicine obtained on the first prescription may have been used. As it is now, he could go to the drug store and have his prescription refilled, but under this Bill he would have to go perhaps twenty or twenty-five miles to a doctor just for the purpose of having another date put on the prescription. I would consider that a great hardship, and I think this difficulty should be eliminated.
I was going to remind the minister that we had legislation of this very character not long ago, and it was referred to a special committee. My hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland) will remember that, because I think he was Chairman of the committee. If the minister would agree to submitting both his Bill and the resolution to a small special committee composed of doctors and druggists, I would have no objection in the world to the resolution passing on that understanding. They could then trim the legislation to meet the circumstances of the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It seems to me that some suggestion of that kind should be carried out, and that it would result in our makifig much greater progress. My suggestion for the time being would be that the resolution be passed, and that the Bill be printed and distributed, and receive its second reading. Then it can be referred to a small special committee to thresh out the details and hear whatever suggestions people who may appear before the committee desire to make.
22C6

Mr. DuTREMBLAY: I see that paragraph 6 provides "for the right of search by any constable or other peace officer who has reasonable cause to suspect that any drug is kept or concealed for any purpose in any premises contrary to the Act." Do I understand that a constable can enter any premises without a sworn complaint first being made? Our criminal law provides that no constable shall enter private premises without having a sworn complaint, and if the constable is to be allowed to enter any premises just on suspicion, I think the consequences will be very disagreeable for the general public.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I cannot agree with the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) that this Bill should be referred to a special committee composed only of doctors and druggists. There are members of the House who are neither doctors or druggists who are interested in this legislation.
I am in entire accord with my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) in regard to this Bill. He has told the committee that he has practised medicine for twenty years, so surely he should know whereof he speaks. I take the same stand that I took last year on legislation- of this character. I think a patient who has received a prescription from his family doctor should have the right to have it refilled as he requires, without having to go back to the doctor and pay $2 for another prescription. It would be a great hardship for people who live in the country to have to go several miles into town to get a doctor to authorize the refilling of a prescription.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: On the other hand, I am sure the hon. member will agree that a drug fiend who gets a prescription from a doctor calling for a large dose of morphine should not have the right to have that prescription refilled by the druggist as often as he pleases. That is the other side of the question. I think there is something in the argument of my hon. friend from Muskoka, and I think it would be* possible for us to find a middle course which would take care of the classes of cases to which he refers. But as for the drug fiend, I think both for his own sake and that of the druggist there should be some provision whereby a prescription calling for large doses of the drug to which he is addicted should not be filled without the approval of the doctor.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have been a druggist long enough, I think, to speak with a little

authority on this question. It is a well-known fact that to-day a good druggist will not refill a prescription containing narcotics without first telephoning the doctor or getting a note from him. I do not see the sense in having so many amendments to the law. I think this particular provision would work a great hardship, and I am very much in favour of what my hon. friend from Muskoka has said. There are cases where a prescription must be refilled. As a rule the physician writes on the prescription " to be filled only once," and the druggist gets in touch with the doctor before refilling it. The druggists are up-to-date, law-abiding citizens who can be trusted to do their duty, and I do not think we should have provisions of this kind, which in my opinion go too far.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The point made by my hon friend is correct, but it is one of the best arguments for the clause. He points out that a good druggist generally communicates with the doctor before refilling a prescription calling for morphine or opium. If that is the case, there is all the more reason wlhy a druggist who is not honest should be compelled to live up to the law and do what the honest druggist does. My hon. friend from North Cape Breton and Victoria pointed out that he did not see any reason why a prescription that was filled for the father of a family should not be used for his child if it had a cold. There, again, is another argument for this clause, for while morphine may safely be given in certain doses to grown-ups, it cannot to young children.
I think the hon. member from Muskoka was a little too strong in his application that the medical men wanted $2 for the refilling of a prescription. As a matter of fact, I do not think there is any class of men in this country wfho do more for charity than do the medical men, including my hon. friend from Muskoka and others. I have never seen this Bill until to-day, but I believe that this clause was put in for the purpose of protecting people from becoming dope fiends, and personally I have heard no arguments why the clause should not be carried.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is it possible to write such a prescription as would prevent a mother from giving to her child medicine which her husband might be taking?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
As I pointed out before, nearly all druggists will re-fill a prescription for the ordinary cough medicine, and it is only where is contains opium or mor-

phine, or some narcotic drug, that they should be required to ring up the doctor on the telephone, which is always practicable, before repeating the prescription. This clause serves to prevent a druggist from enabling an otherwise honest man or woman to become a dope fiend by getting too large doses of morphine or opium. The ordinary prescription can be refilled without difficulty. As regards the patient whose pitiful plight has been depicted, who has to drive seven or ten, or fifteen miles to a doctor's office, I do not think that there is any difficulty that might not be easily overcome. After all, there is a telephone system in practically every part of the country.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Well, in very many parts of the country, at any rate, and I am safe in saying that there is telephone connection between every drug store and the doctors; and in the refilling of prescriptions the telephone is made use of in a large proportion of cases.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is it a fact that most cough medicines contain narcotics?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No, it is not.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I may remind the member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) that his clause prevents refilling by telephone conversation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If the suggestion that
has been made is to be carried out, I think we might postpone further discussion at the present time, because the whole matter will have to be gone over again. If we pass the resolution now, and afterwards refer the Bill to a special committee, I think we might very well, at this stage, postpone the discussion of the subject. I agree with the member for Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) that if we constitute a committee of the kind suggested, it should not be composed entirely of doctors, but others should be represented.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Will the minister explain clause 2?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This clause provides that physicians shall not be allowed to sell narcotic drugs except for medicinal purposes, on order or prescription. I am advised by the officers of the department that there are a certain number of physicians throughout the country who commercialize in this business. They secure fairly large quantities of these drugs, as they have a right to do, but instead of dispensing them on prescription to
patients, they simply make a business of selling to drug addicts, and the object of the clause is to put an end to that practice. The physician who disposes of these drugs must do so only on prescription; that is the sole object of the proposed amendment.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Will the doctor in the
country not be able to supply drugs to his patients without prescription to be filled by a druggist?

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friend will
understand-

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Let the minister explain it.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have no objection to
allowing the minister to answer the question, but I could give the hon. member an explanation.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I understood from the
minister's remarks that a doctor would not be able to furnish these drugs to his own patients without first having a prescription filled by a druggist.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Then will the minister
explain the clause more fully?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I should imagine that
where a doctor himself sells these drugs he must keep a record of his prescriptions. I am not quite certain as to that point, but I think that is the provision of the law. My impression is that if the doctor sells these drugs he must have a record of each sale in the form of a prescription which can be checked by the officers of the law.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: A prescription which he may fill himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do not think that the law does provide that the doctor shall keep such a record. I know that when we were discussing the matter last year it was provided that druggists should keep a record, but I am pretty certain that there was nothing that compelled the doctor to do the same. The suggestion was made, but I do not think it was carried.

maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The object of this Bill is to prevent persons who have a tendency towards the drug habit from becoming what are known as dope fiends. If a man has a broken leg, in the United States, under the Harrison Act there must be a record if he is given a quarter of a grain or half a grain of morphine. We do not



need such restrictions in Canada. This resolution covers that point, for it provides that no drugs shall be given except for medicinal purposes, and on prescription. I remember a case in one of the cities in Canada where a doctor was approached by a drug fiend and offered a fabulous sum for an ounce of morphine. The doctor proceeded to procure the drug, but by a very ingenious trick on the part of the "patient" he was nicely taken in. He had arranged to meet his client at a hotel, and after delivering the drug, he was instructed to go to another room to receive the price of the sale; but when he went there was nobody there, and, of course, he did hot get the money he expected. The drug ring to-day is the greatest menace we have to contend with in Canada. Winnipeg is one of the important centres for the distribution of drugs, and, according to this morning's papers, $35,000 worth of drugs, which would have been sold at double that figure, were caught on one of the chief men in the drug ring in Toronto. Now, these restrictions cannot be made too stringent if we are to stamp out the drug traffic. The provision that no prescription shall be used more than once is, I think, necessary and wise, because in the large cities certain people have acquired the drug habit, and if they were allowed to refill a prescription indefinitely you might as well abandon any attempt to control the traffic. The suggestion that this resolution will work a hardship on those people who obtain cough medicines has nc weight, in my opinion. I cannot recall, in the course of my practice last year, any case in which such a prescription has been filled more than twice, and it is easy to renew the order. I do not think, therefore, that there will be any hardship on anyone. We must restrict the sale of these drugs, and to do so we must prevent the indiscriminate use of them. I have gone over these amendments with the officers of the Health Department, whose explanations are entirely satisfactory. In connection with almost every Act, some loopholes are always discovered after the Act has operated a certain time, and steps should be taken without delay, to repair them and make the law as workable as possible. I do not think that more than once or twice in a large practice will there be found any case of real hardship from the operation of section 1.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: Will the suggestion I have made regarding the matter of sworn complaint be embodied in the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: OPIUM AND NARCOTIC DRUG ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The whole matter will be subject to further discussion. If the Bill goes to a special committee that committee will consider all its provisions and it will be reported back to the House, and will go through Committee of the Whole in the usual way. The passing of the resolution now does not necessarily mean that its exact terms will be finally embodied in the legislation that will be passed by the House.
Resolution reported.
Hon. Mr. Calder thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 81, founded on the resolution, to amend the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

If any person acts in contravention of this section, or acts in contravention of or fails to comply with any condition attached to a license granted under this section, he shall, for each offence, be liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds, or to imprisonment with or without hard labour for a term not exceeding two years, or to both such fine and imprisonment, and in addition to any other punishment, the court dealing with the case may order the articles in respect of which the offence was committed to be forfeited.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the motion of Hon. Mr. Guthrie for Committee of Supply:

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: ['Under protest and on division.']

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day were proceeded with this afternoon I endeavoured to direct the attention of the Government and of the minister to whose department the matter related to a return brought down in this House on the 11th of this month, marked Sessional Papers No. 131. The return is obviously incorrect and misleading and there are omitted from it certain papers which should have been brought down and which have an important bearing on the matter to which I am referring.
On the 15th of March last, when the Estimates of the Department of Agricul-. ture were before the House, I referred to the case of the destruction of a large herd of hogs by a Government inspector. The owner of these animals has been unable to get any compensation for the loss sustained under the Act providing for such cases. Just about one column of Hansard was taken up with my remarks on that occasion. On the 17th of the same month the minister brought the matter up again when his Estimates were before the House and referred to it at considerable length, and it was the subject of a good deal of discussion on that occasion. From the remarks made by the minister I felt that the only recourse I had was to place a notice of motion on the Order Paper asking that all the papers in connection with the matter be brought down and laid on the table of the House. This I did, and in response to that motion, moved on the 8th of this month, the return referred to was tabled. As I said at the outset, it is quite obvious that the return is not complete and that it contains matter quite uncalled for in a return of this nature. I refer to a memorandum attached to it, unsigned and undated, which

endeavours to give a synopsis of the whole case, but which is biased and incorrect, as I can easily demonstrate by some reports of inspectors given in the return. It is with a good deal of reluctance that I feel it necessary to bring this matter before the House and to take up the time of Parliament in this way.
It will be one year to-morrow since the inspectors arrived on the premises of this man, Mr. George B. Alderson, and destroyed his herd of 245 hogs. He has from that time to the present been endeavouring to secure some consideration, but without avail, and in view of the statement made by the minister on March 17 last, which indicated that he had evidently closed the case, I feel that there is no other recourse than to bring the matter before Parliament because aparently no other means are open to Mr. Alderson to have his grievance ventilated and the documents relating to the case produced.
The return, as I have stated, is obviously incorrect and misleading, as may be seen from the memorandum attached to it. Page 49 of the return contains what purports to be an application for license signed by Mr. Alderson. I have a copy of the application which was signed by Mr. Alderson and it is quite different from the one which is found in the return. The application brought down in the return contains this provision:
1. To boil thoroughly all garbage before feeding it to swine, and to prevent my swine from having access to uncooked garbage.
This was not contained in the application made and signed by the applicant for the license. The application which he signed also contained a provision which is not to be found in that brought down in the return. That this was apparent to the Veterinary Director General is quite evident from the report he submitted to the minister under date of March the 19th in answer to a personal request I made of the minister some time before, in which he gives an outline of the correct application. Now, this has a very important bearing on the whole matter, because at the outset the inspector endeavoured to make it appear that Mr. Alderson was aware of the fact that his animals were diseased and that they had been dying from disease. He claimed that he was not aware of it; that he had not lost any as a result of disease; that all the animals were taking their feed regularly and that he was unaware of any disease until the inspector came around and

condemned them. Now, this is referred to in the memorandum which is attached, and which says:
If disease was so evident to the eye of an untrained observer like the garbage inspector, why should the owner not notice it? The probability is that he knew the hogs were sick but neglected to notify our office.
The inspector in his report-page 31 of the return-states that when he made the examination of the herd, Dr. Tennant, another inspector, accompanied him on his inspection of the premises. So that the garbage inspector was not really alone; he was accompanied by a veterinary inspector of the department. After considerable correspondence and after having been notified by the Veterinary Director General that no compensation could be paid to him unless he could show that the disease had been introduced into his herd from some outside source, it would be assumed that the disease had occurred through the feeding of garbage, and he would not be entitled to any compensation. Mr. Alderson, claimed that he was unaware of the existence of any disease in his herd. After receiving this notice from the inspector, and when it was made quite evident that unless he could show that disease had been introduced from some outside source he would receive no compensation, he in a letter dated September 21, which is included in the report, stated that he was enclosing a list of names of those who had hogs on his premises about the time that the trouble occurred. This list is not included in the return. Mr Alderson claims that the person referred to, R. H. Parker, had lost all the animals . which he had on Mr. Alderson's premises shortly before the trouble arose. Upon receipt of this letter the Veterinary Director General notified the office of the Veterinary Department in Toronto-page 24 of return -4n charge of Mr. Moynihan, and referred to the statement contained in Mr. Aider-son's letter; but he refrained from notifying Mr. Moynihan of the case Mr. Aider-son had referred to-that of Mr. R. H. Parker. He gave him the names of those who, Mr. Alderson admitted, had hogs on his premises and who had not lost any hogs, but he refrained from giving to inspector Moynihan of Toronto, when he asked that a further inquiry be made into, the matter, the one case-that of Mr. R.
H.	Parker-in which Mr. Alderson pointed out that he had lost all the hogs that had been on his premises. Mr. Moynihan evidently instructed Mr. Richards, who had made the inspection of the premises in the
first instance, to make a further examination and Mr. Richards' report is contained in this return-pages 40 and 41. In that report he says:
Mr. Alderson Sr. was absent but his son, who was in charge of the hogs at time of outbreak, was interviewed this date and he advises me that the only hogs that he had any knowledge of being on his premises at any recent date prior to outbreak were from the premises of R.
H. Parker. See separate report under his name.
The House will observe that the Veterinary Director General withheld the name of Mr. Parker in asking to have an investigation made. Incidentally, Mr. Richards, who was making the investigation, found from the information which he obtained from Mr. Alderson's son, that, in the case of Mr. Parker, hogs had died, and he evidently made a separate report which he refers to in his report to the head of the branch. This had also been withheld, and it is not contained in this return.
Further on in the correspondence the Veterinary Director General, after having taken the stand that it would be necessary to establish by reasonable proof that the hogs might have acquired the disease by contact or otherwise, in order to obtain compensation, departs from that stand and claims that the man should have notified the department as soon as sickness broke out amongst his animals. It was quite apparent that the man could not notify the inspector if he was not aware that his animals were sick. Let us see what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) had to say on the matter when I brought it up on a former occasion in the House. He informed the House that he himself had been one of those veterinary inspectors. He s.tated:
Hog cholera is not a disease which shows itself very clearly in all cases. Where the disease is very acute the animal dies within a few hours and the symptoms are clearly defined; but . should the animal be suffering from chronic cholera there would be no external symptoms and to the eye of the layman the hog would be apparently healthy. So far as our Health of Animals branch is concerned, I want to say that It is the most efficient, not merely on this con-titnent, but in the whole world.
The House will observe that the minister himself said that the disease might be present in a herd and an ordinary layman not be aware of the fact. On the next occasion when the matter came before the House, the minister was very emphatic, and he called attention to a statement which I had made on March 15. He said:,
Then, again, the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) criticised the Health

of Animals Branch on account of their action in connection with an outbreak of hog- cholera on the farm of one Alderson. He stated that Alderson said that his hogs were not infected with hog cholera and were free from disease. I am quite sure that the hon. gentleman was not fully informed or he would not have made the statement. In the first place, the ordinary garbage inspector who was sent down to inspect these hogs-this being a garbage feeding plant [DOT]-had no difficulty whatever i.n diagnosing the disease among those hogs as hog cholera. He immediately advised the Health of Animals Branch inspectors; a careful inspection was made, and they had no difficulty in confirming the lay inspector's diagnosis.
I have pointed out that the lay inspector's report shows that he was accompanied by a veterinary surgeon, one of the inspectors of the department, on the occasion when he visited the premises. Evidently the case is closed and no compensation is forthcoming, because on that occasion the minister stated:
These men are experts in their particular line., I worked fourteen years in this profession. I was chief inspector for British Columbia for that length of time, handled hundreds of cases of hog cholera and am fairly familiar with the details. Hence, I consider myself fairly efficient to form a judgment in such matters, as compared with the average hog owner	It is
a very interesting story that the hon. member (Mr. Sutherland) has told to-night-very interesting indeed. I have heard it time and time again west of the Rocky Mountains.
A little further on, referring to Dr. Hall, he said:
Dr. Hall, a man who has been in the service for twelve or thirteen years, and whose word I would take any day of the week before I would take that of a man who Was not qualified and had not received the proper training of an inspector. How are we going to carry out the requirements of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act in this country if we cannot rely on our inspectors?
A little further on he said:
How are we ever going to keep disease out of the country, and maintain the enviable position we now enjoy in regard to contagious disease, if we are going to turn down the statement of our experts and accept the word of the hog owner? The mere fact that only thirty-three out of two hundred and thirty-five hogs were found free from disease, is an indication that there certainly was hog cholera in that herd.
A little further on:
Yet we know that our inspectors are reliable men who have been in the service for a long time, there is no reason to think they did not tell the truth, and until the opposite can be proved we are bound to accept their word. The owners of those hogs broke the rule not only in failing to cook the garbage thoroughly, but also in not reporting that the disease existed on their premises, and therefore they forfeited their right to compensation.
The minister evidently had been informed of this matter only a very short 
time previously by the officers of his department; in fact, I know that he had no personal knowledge of the fact until I called his attention to it just a short time before the matter came up in the House. He has evidently placed too great confidence in the officers in his department, because when he states that none of the other animals that were slaughtered were fit for food, he is making a statement that. I think he will find it very difficult to prove if these men are given an opportunity to have their case properly tried and investigated.
Inspector Richards' report shows that the 33 hogs that were segregated and which Mr. Alderson had permission to slaughter were suspected of being infected with the disease as well as the others. See report by Richards, pages 34 and 35. Mr. Aledrson picked them out of the different pens, and he makes a declaration that the temperature of eight of those that were slaughtered had been taken by the inspector when he was on the premises and declared to have a high temperature. You will find from the report of Inspector Richards that he makes the statement that he suspected the animals were diseased, and when the officers of his department tried to make it appear that these animals were apparently free from disease and that the others were so badly diseased that they were not fit for food, they are making a statement that they will find it hard to substantiate. On the first occasion when I brought this matter before the House, in the few remarks that I made, I pointed out that all that this man was asking was to have a fair and proper investigation made into the matter by a commission or otherwise, and that he was prepared to accept the verdict, but he does not feel inclined to submit to being ruined without a protest. For a man over* seventy years of age, who had put every dollar he had in this business, who had invested nearly $10,000 in the pens where he was breeding the hogs and who estimated that between seven and eight thousand dollars' worth of animals were destroyed on that occasion, to be dealt with in this arbitrary way is, it will be readily admitted, a great hardship. The 33 animals which were slaughtered and dressed and disposed of by Mr. Alderson as fit for food were all passed by the inspector. They were killed on the premises and hung up there. The intestines were left lying beside each animal, the inspector examined every one carefully, and failed to find any evidence of disease in any one of the animals that had been slaughtered.

A great ado is being made about Mr. Al-derson's son having admitted that they had lost a number of animals, and that consequently they must have been aware of the disease. Mr. Alderson's son, Mr. Alder-son himself, and his foreman all declare most emphatically that they had not lost a hog from disease or in any other way, but that a number of small pigs had died during the winter, not from disease, but from accident and other causes.
I do not wish to take up any more of the time of the House in connection with this matter, but what I do desire is that the return to the Order of the House shall be a correct one, because it will be necessary, if there is no other recourse open to Mr. Alderson, to ask for a fiat to enable him to sue and endeavour to establish his case in the courts. That may be necessary and it will be preferable to having his case disposed of in the arbitrary and autocratic manner in which it evidently has been handled. I do not think that the framers of the Act under which compensation is allowed for animals that are destroyed ever contemplated such high-handed action as was taken by the inspectors in this case. It is a very easy matter for these men who are supposed to be experts to take a stand on a question, and apparently there is no recourse but to accept their decision. They get away with many things in this way and they do it in a manner that would not be allowed if the case were tried in court.
I have touched upon some of the features of this case. I have pointed out some of the inaccuracies, omissions, and misrepresentations contained in this return. When this House passes an order for a return to be placed on the Table, we naturally expect that the return will be a correct one, and that the whole correspondence in connection with the matter will be placed before Parliament. I might read the motion for the papers, which was made on April 8:
A copy of all reports, orders, telegrams, certificates of valuation, or any other correspondence relating to or connected with the slaughter of 245 hogs the property of one George B. Alderson, hy officers of the Department of Agriculture on or about the 20th day of April, 1920, and for which compensation has been refused by the minister.
You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that the terms of the motion were broad, and that there can be no excuse whatever for withholding any of the information in connection with this matter that is in the department. I believe that my request is a reasonable one. It may be necessary for
me to bring this question up again unless something is done. In the meantime, I want to see that all the evidence that is in the Department of Agriculture in connection with the subject is laid on the Table, so that this man will know exactly what has been done. I might say that the man who made a post mortem examination of one small pig has apparently not made a report on his examination at all. - It is referred to by the garbage inspector, and by another, but as far as Dr. Hall is concerned there is not one word in the return to indicate that he ever found disease in the animal upon which he held the post mortem.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton and Victoria) :
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when so worthy a representative as the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) makes such a serious statement as he has done to the House this evening, one expects some reply from the Prime Minister, or from some one representing the Department of Agriculture, against which department this most serious charge is made. I say most serious, Mr. Speaker, because any tampering with the records of this House, or any refusal on the part of any official of the Government to comply with an order of the House of Commons, must always be regarded as most serious.
The hon. member for South Oxford points out that on a, certain day an order passed this House calling upon the Department of Agriculture to bring down all the records in connection with this hog cholera case. I do not think my hon. friend has done full justice to himself in that he has not pointed out where these mistakes, misrepresentations, and inaccuracies are in the return, but as a private member of the House I must accept his word that there are misrepresentations, mistakes, and inaccuracies in the return that has been brought down to Parliament. I am not going to elaborate that point, Mr. Speaker, beyond saying that it is a great pity that the confidence of the House should be shaken to the extent that the language of the hon. member must have shaken it with reference to returns of this character. We have a right to expect that every single item of evidence in the possession of the department in connection with this matter will be brought down in response to an order of this kind. If there is anything of a confidential nature that should not be brought down, the minister, when he is laying the return on the Table should

say: I have brought down everything that I can bring down but there are some things of a confidential nature which cannot be brought down. Sometimes the minister will tell, an hon. member who has moved for papers that he can have access to confidential documents privately. This matter should not be allowed to pass unnoticed, for the reasons I have already given. There are a great many lawyers m this House and the practice of their profession has taught them the sacredness with which all records of a court are regarded. If a prothonotary or a clerk of the court was suspected of tampering with the records, taking out a man s defence and putting in a different one, or taking out a man's writ and statement of claim and substituting another or destroying them altogether, how long would the barristers and the judges of this country put up with tampering of that kind? The ordinary court is but a small affair compared with the House of Commons. The House of Commons is the supreme court of them all, and the records of the departments are the records of this court. They are to be correctly filed, and they should be accurate in every particular, so far as any human institution can be accurate; and when the House of Commons, with all its force and solemnity, passes an order calling on any of the departments to bring down reports, it should not be regarded as a trivial matter if those reports prove to be, as the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) states, inaccurate and misleading, something being omitted altogether from the information submitted. While personally I have no interest in the world in this matter, I do say that for the peace, order and good government of the House of Commons it is of the highest importance that we should all have confidence in the departments and in their officials.
I therefore submit to the Prime Minister that a proper investigation should be instituted into this matter and that, when he is fully seized of the facts in connection with it, he should inform the House as to the true situation and endeavour to have remedied any difficulty that may exist.
As to the question of a fiat, we in this House have nothing to do with that; it has no business being raised here. The Department of the Secretary of State, I believe, deals with the questions of fiats. The matter first goes before that Department and thence it is taken to the Department of Justice. I think that is the condition now; at all events, the question is !IMr. McKenzie.]
one of detail, not for this House. If a man presents a petition showing a good case he generally gets the fiat, but the House of Commons has nothing whatever to do with that question. It is only a matter of $2 to obtain the fiat. My hon. friend is not a lawyer and therefore is not familiar with the steps one should take to get a fiat. However, without charging him anything, I now inform him of the proper course to pursue, and if his friend has a good case he will know what to do. As to the other matter, it is one entirely of public concern, and I do, with all sincerity, submit to the Prime Minister that a case of this kind should not pass unnoticed. I have been in this House a good number of years and I cannot recall any instance of this kind before, where an Order of the House calling for papers has been met with the charge, made by the mover of the motion, that the papers brought down are not in accordance with the Order, but are erroneous, deceptive and misleading. If such is the case, it certainly Should be inquired into.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The minister of the department concerned is not in his place to-night, and I have no doubt the reason is that he did not know that this subject was to be brought up. As I understand the complaint, it is that some papers brought down in answer to a motion are not in some respects_ correct; and, as well, that the papers include a memorandum, evidently prepared by the department, summarizing the case from the departmental standpoint. As to the latter, that would, I would presume, be the right of the department if they so chose. There could be no objection on the part of any one to the department doing more than the order of the House called for. There could, of course, be objection if the return filed were not in accordance with the order of the House; and as to that, I will request that the speech of the hon. member be read and compared with the return in order to ascertain whether or not the return is in any respect in error or is not fully in accordance with the order of the House. As to fiat, that of course is a subject for application to the Secretary of State, who in turn submits it to the Department of Justice. The rules of the department as to the granting of fiats are very well known; they are not reviewed by the Governor General in Council.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
