maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Last evening, at the beginning of the discussion, I called the attention of the minister to the status of certain members of the Permanent Force of Canada whose salaries had been deducted in order that the deductions might be applied to the pension fund, and who, on demobilization, were refused a refund of the sums deducted. I now have before me the facts of one particular case, and I should like an explanation from the minister regarding this matter.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I do not know that'I can add anything to the explanation I gave last night. The members of the Permanent Force, of commissioned and noncommissioned rank, contribute a certain percentage of their pay to the pension fund. If they fulfil their term of service, they are entitled to pension; if they do not serve their term, they receive, in lieu of pension, one month's gratuity for each year of service. This applies only to warrant officers and officers of the Permanent Force. The ranks of the Permanent Force beneath warrant officers do not contribute to the pension fund. If money has been paid into the pension fund it has gone to the Receiver General, and, so far as I am aware, there is no way of getting it back under the present statute, which provides that the money shall go to the credit of the fund. I do not know what further explanation my hon. friend desires. If he will be more explicit, I shall try to give him any further information I can.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
It is admitted by the Department of Militia that certain deductions were made from the salaries of officers and non-commissioned officers during the war. As the minister is well aware, all members of the Permanent Force became members of the Canadian Expeditionary F'wce also at a certain period of the war; that we have members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force from whose salaries a certain percentage was deducted by the Government. When we ask to obtain a refund of this money the minister tells me that unfortunately it has been paid to such and such
a department of Government and that we cannot obtain a refund. Without understanding particularly the technical phases of the situation it seems to me that the broad question is this: If the man had some money deducted from his pay and allowances he should get it back. If there is no other way of giving it to him give him a sufficient gratuity; take advantage of the Audit Act, or whatever statute governs a case like this. Surely the Government can find means to pay the money which it owes, since it pays thousands of dollars which it does not owe. I would like the minister to give a more satisfactory explanation than to tell the House: "Yes, we owe the money but we cannot pay it." If the minister cannot give me that satisfactory explanation I would like him to tell me how many men have cases of this kind, if he knows. Then we will take such proceedings as the situation seems to call for.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I may say in the first place that the Government does not owe the money in any sense of the word. I think my hon. friend knows that the Permanent Force at the time of the war was merged in the Canadian Expeditionary Force. Those of the Permanent Force in Canada who were of the rank of warrant officer or commissioned officer are entitled under our law to pensions at the end of their period of service-formerly twenty years, now ten years. A certain amount was annually deducted from the pay of the Permanent Force and up to the time of the war that pension fund cost the treasury of Canada nothing-it was self sustaining. The Permanent Force was then merged in the1 Canadian Expeditionary Force, and the pay in the Canadian Expeditionary Force was higher than the old Permanent Force pay. The men of the Permanent Force were still charged the five per cent on the Permanent Force pay, not on the Canadian Expeditionary Force pay. That was deducted and put to the credit of the pension fund. Now it so happened that the pay of all the officers of the Permanent Force throughout the country was charged to the Permanent Force vote; only their excess pay was charged to the Canadian Expeditionary Force vote. Had these men continued in the Permanent Force they would have enjpyed their pensions, but they did not remain.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: You demobilized them?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Not without consulting them. There are only between sixty

and seventy all told, and if a man was demobilized-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: You could not pay him.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: We did pay him one month's gratuity for each month's service. Now that is the law and you cannot get away from it. If Parliament changes the statute I suppose there might be a remedy, but that is the law under which these men enlisted and joined the Permanent Force and it must be presumed they knew the law. I cannot see that there is any debt owing to these men, or any liability on the part of the Government towards them. If the House saw fit to change the statute, I suppose they could be repaid, but that money is trust money to support that pension fund.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I agree with the minister that perhaps this man obtained his gratuity, but as a member of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, which he became by Order in Council, he obtained a gratuity anyway.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: He got his war service gratuity as well. I did not mention that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: He got his war service gratuity as well?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Did the gratuity which he obtained amount to as much as he had paid into the pension fund?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: No, not quite. He paid five per cent per annum on his salary and he got back one month's allowance for each month he had served by way of gratuity, and in addition got six months" war gratuity.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Which he was entitled to as a member of the Canadian Expeditionary Force.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I did not mention that because he got it as his right.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The point is this: He paid a certain amount of money to the Government of Canada for certain service but the Government, owing to no fault of his own, did not give him a pension. He is demobilized now and it seems to me that in all justice and reason he and the others should get their money back. I cannot for the life of me understand the explanation given bjr the minister in which he says, "We cannot give this money back to him." Surely, if the money is owed, there is some means whereby the Government can give it
TMr. Guthrie.]
back. The minister does not deny that the money is due.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I do deny it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Well, the minister does
not deny the man paid in a certain amount of money.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: No, I do not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The minister admits that the man paid to the Government a certain amount of money for a certain service, namely a pension. The minister also admits that the man did not get this service. Surely by all the rules of justice he is entitled to get his money back. He has paid that money in but he does not get it back. I cannot understand why some means is not taken to give it to him.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I do not know that I
can make the matter any more plain. I have tried to demonstrate as clearly as I could that a man who joins the permanent force is presumed to know the law. There is the provision in the statute and as soon as he joins-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
This man joined during
the war.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Before the war, or
during the war, or since the war, it does not matter. The statute has not be6n changed. There is the law, the man knows when he joins that a certain amount of his pay is deducted annually for the purposes of his pension, and while he is in the force he receives the protection which the pension fund gives him. Now every man who joins the permanent force knows that he is liable to be discharged-that is a rule in the army. The men are supposed to know that. As a matter of fact we did not discharge them, but at the end of the recent war if certain men were let out it was because we had such a splendid lot of excellent men. Many of them had risen from the ranks to high command but it was impossible to retain the services of them all. Unfortunately we had to let some of them go, but to any that were let go we paid a gratuity for each month's service and in addition six months' war gratuity. I cannot see any more that can be done. If the House choses to change the laws and orders the money to be paid I suppose it will be paid, but in the meantime the Auditor General will not pay the money on the order of anybody that I know of.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
My suggestion is that if
the minister recognizes the justice of the

claim he ought to use his influence with his colleagues.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I do not recognize that there is any just claim that has not been paid. I do not recognize that there is any grievance at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
In that case the minister's sense of justice and mine are different. I had expected rather more of him. However, this man states definitely, and is under the impression, that the Militia Department owes him some money. He says here:
It matters not to me whether this money has been placed in the Consolidated Revenue fund of Canada or anywhere else. But what does matter is this: is it to be refunded?
That to me is as plain a statement as any one can make. He says he has paid money and he wants it back. The minister says he does not recognize the justice of this claim. In that event there is nothing more for us to do; there is no resolution or motion which I can make in this case.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
What was the rank of
the man?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
He is a captain, but it
does not make very much difference what he was.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: What was he at the outbreak of the war?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I have not the man's
record; I cannot tell the minister what he was. Whether he was a boot-black or anything of that kind does not matter to me. The point is that he served in the army and gave his money to the Government but did not get it back. That is the only question in which I am interested. Of course, if the minister refuses to enter into any further discussion of the matter, I can only leave it as it is.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I do not at all refuse
to enter into a discussion. But the point that my hon. friend is making is that there is a debt of obligation and if he could make the matter any more clear to me I would be only too glad to listen, and reconsider it. My hon. friend must not say that the minister persists in refusing to recognize a just claim when I am satisfied there is no valid claim.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Is there not a debt of
honour.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Perhaps you could call it that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Just before the committee adjourned last night I asked the
Minister of Militia a question with regard to dispensing with the services of a man named Douglas and the minister made a rather peculiar reply. This is what he said:
There was in that branch a man named Douglas, whose services were dispensed with for certain reasons which I will give to my hon. friend after adjournment if that will suit him.
Well, the House adjourned so quickly that I did not have a chance to say whether it suited me or not. I want to say now that it does not suit me. Charges have been made that funds were misappropriated, that certain persons' services were dispensed with, and that the matter had been hushed up. I think the minister's reply last night is very good evidence of that. He is ready to give a member the information privately, but he refuses to give that information on the floor of the House, where members should receive it. Does the minister wish to shield somebody higher up, or just what is the reason that he refused to give this information to the House last night?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I think my hon. friend's insinuation is rather strange, because I explained to him everything about the Douglas case. Douglas was one of those guilty of irregularities in the pay office. He left the country hastily. Several charges were preferred against him of having forged the names of soldiers to the endorsements upon their war service gratuity cheques. It was said that he was in Texas at one time, and in New York at another time. Unfortunately, the man has a family and a father in town, and it was for that reason that I did not wish to mention the matter last night, but I gave full particulars to my hon. friend this afternoon.	,

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Will those claims
have to be paid over again by the Militia Department?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: No, the department is not a loser; the liability, is against the bank for having paid the forged cheques. As a matter of fact, some of the relatives of the defaulter undertook to dispose of what little household furniture he had and brought the proceeds to the department. That money was paid over to the Receiver-General, and the whole matter is in the hands of the Justice Department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I do not quite understand the hon. minister. In one breath he

says that the department was not a loser, and that the bank was liable; in the next breath he says that the proceeds of the furniture were paid to the department and by the department paid over to the Receiver-General on account of this man's defalcations. If the bank was out of pocket, why was the money refunded to the department?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The money was handed to the Militia Department, and the Militia Department handed it over to the Receiver-General. The whole matter is now in the hands of the Justice Department. I believe creditors are claiming the money, and that the bank is also claiming it, but the Militia Department is not making any claim to it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Under this item is the minister prepared to discuss the question of militia pensions?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Probably this is just as good an item as any to discuss that question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Is there any special item for military hospitals?
_ Mr. POWER: I wish to refer to the pensions being received by men who were wounded in the South African war or while on active service in Canada. I am not referring now to the long service pensions. I have a case before me of a man who was discharged from the army as absolutely medically unfit owing to disability incurred on service during the South African war. He is totally deaf. He draws a total pension of $6 per month. I do not wish _ to increase the expenditure of the Militia Department, but does not the minister feel that something can be done for these men-and there are a considerable number of them-who are suffering from war disabilities? I think they might well be transferred to the Board of Pension Commissioners to be dealt with as C.E.F.
cases. After all, this man whose 9 p.m. case I have cited suffered equally _ in the service of his country as a man disabled in the recent war and he should have the same claim to a pension. The officers in the old Permanent Force have been very well looked after indeed; in fact, the Permanent Force, as far as I know, was principally for the officers. But the N.C.O.'s and men have not fared so well, and I would urge on the minister the importance of obtaining an increase for those who have really suffered from the 
disabilities incurred during war service. I feel certain the minister could find some means of doing this if he would only take the matter up with the proper authorities.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I think the matter should receive the sympathetic consideration of the House. There is a tremendous discrepancy between the South African pensions and the pensions awarded in respect of the late war. Conditions twenty odd years ago were very different from what they are to-day, and I have no doubt that when the South African pensions were awarded they were considered fair and equitable. However, this matter will require further consideration, and I am glad to say that it is now, I believe, before a special committee of this House known as the Soldiers' Re-establishment Committee which is dealing with all such cases. This question, I believe, will be considered1 and a report presented to the House by that committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I am very glad to hear the minister state that some consideration is goipg to be given to our men who fought in the defence of their country many years ago. We still have a few veterans of the Fenian raid and the Crimean war who are to-day really in need of assistance, and it seems to me that their cases are deserving of sympathetic consideration. These men who in the past served their country so faithfully should to-day in their old age be relieved from want, and I hope the minister will see if some assistance cannot be given to men whp deserve so well of their country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: With reference to the item under consideration, is the amount required for the Record Office to be found on page 76 or page 77?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I do not know that it is in separate form anywhere in the Estimates.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I would like to know
what the Record Office cost.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: While that information is being looked up, might I for my own information ask what is the strength of the permanent force?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Non-commissioned
ranks, 3,865; commissioned ranks, 447.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
But was the department
not empowered by statute the year before last to increase the standing army, if I may so call it, to 10,000?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Power was given by
the statute to increase it should it become necessary to do so, but it was determined soon after the Act was passed not to increase it beyond 5,000. Subsequently it was decided not to go beyond 4,000. We have not yet reached the 4,000 limit. I do not know that there is any immediate need of going further, but if the need should arise the power is there in the statute.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The argument made by
the Opposition two years ago when the Bill was before the House was evidently a good one. What happened at that particular time to cause the department to ask for an increase from 5,000 to 10,000?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
We were either in war
or very recently out of war and our ideas were, perhaps, a bit enlarged and inflamed by reason of the fact that we had raised nearly half a million men for the Great War and 10,000 looked like a very insignificant number. I am glad that we have not found it necessary to go beyond the
4.000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The department found
that we had defeated our enemy with half a million men, and though there was really no danger at that particular time, it was deemed necessary, owing to the inflamed condition of our imagination, to increase the strength of the force from 5,000 to
10.000.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Of course, the Permanent Force is essentially a training force. It is a first-class fighting force, too, but its first purpose is to train the Canadian militia.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
This training force of
3,500 was able to train half a million men to send across the sea during the war; therefore I conclude that 10,000 would be able to train something like a million and a half.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I have no doubt that
for twenty or thirty years the permanent force had done a tremendous amount of valuable training of the militia unit^ of Canada, and when the war broke out the effect of that training was immediately seen. But the Permanent Force did not train the half million men that went to the front.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
What was the strength
of the Permanent Force before the war?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
2,970, the last year,
I think, before the war.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I understood that Military District No. 12 was formed to meet the war needs and that it was to be dispensed with. Is it still in existence?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: There was at one time a suggestion that the military district in Saskatchewan with headquarters at Regina might be dispensed with and the command taken over either at Winnipeg or at Calgary. But it turned out subsequently that Saskatchewan was one of the finest recruiting areas for the militia in Canada, and as the amount involved was not very substantial it was thought that it would be well to maintain the district headquarters at Regina. Saskatchewan has a very large body of militiamen who require training.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Why is it, then, that we
have no rifle range or military barracks or anything else of the kind in that district?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The reason is that we
have not the money to build them. I would like very much to be able to announce that' we are going ahead with the construction of necessary barracks for the permanent force, drill halls for the militia, and rifle ranges for our infantry regiments. But in preparing the Militia Estimates this year we cut down as closely as possible and we have very little for rifle ranges and nothing for drill halls or barracks.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I have compiled some
figures from the Auditor General's Report of last year, and if the same condition obtains in all the military districts of Canada as obtains in Military District No. 12, perhaps a means may be found whereby the minister may procure the necessary moneys to build all the rifle ranges and barracks required in these districts. The totals which I have arrived at are somewhat different from those given in the Auditor General's Report. I find that the amount required for Military Distrct No. 12 was $105,704.52, divided as follows:	officers' salaries,
$41,769.50; non-commissioned officers and men, salaries, provisions, etc., $63,305.02. Now, I thought that $41,000 odd was a very large amount to spend in the administration of a business the work of which that $63,000 would pay for. Further, I took the liberty of adding to the item of officers' salaries one-thirteenth of the pay of the headquarters' staff here, counting it all as administration expenses. When I did that, the total amount required to carry on work which $63,305.02 would pay for, was found to be $72,987.75. Now, if a condition similar to that obtains in each military dis-

triet, the taxpayers are being called upon to pay something that they should not have to pay. It would seem that a reorganization or readjustment might give the minister enough money to enable him to build the necessary rifle ranges and barracks so that he would not have to pay exorbitant rates for the rental of buildings to house the men. The active militia in Saskatchewan is not very great at this time; in fact, the bulk of the information which I receive from Military District No. 12 indicates that there is one officer for every two men out there. Some of these officers receive large remuneration, having the benefit of a private car, chauffeur and so on. It is unfair to the people, having regard to the conditions of taxation at present prevailing, that exorbitant salaries should be paid to large numbers of officers. I would refer the minister to the remarks of my respected leader during the debate on the Address, to the effect that we should have retrenchment. I think that there is opportunity irt these Estimates for the exercise of retrenchment. If the minister accepted the advice tendered by my leader on that occasion he would pare these Estimates right down to the bone. The reduction of approximately $50,000 made last night before adjournment did not satisfy me; if the matter was looked into carefully it would be found that the militia of Canada would not suffer materially if the proposed appropriations were cut well-nigh in half. I would support any resolution presented by an hon. member for a decrease of the expenditure to that extent. It is a well known fact in this House that I am not a militarist; yet I wish to place myself on record because I have received so many advices and communications from my people asking me to take this stand. I take it in all sincerity and on my own initiative, but I know that I am representing the people of Saskatchewan, a province, which, I am pleased to say, received such a high recommendation from the minister to-night.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Has the minister his reply to my question ready?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The amount of this Estimate that pertains to the Record Office is $85,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Is that the total cost of the Record Office?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
There is the rent of buildings and the temporary clerks whom we are letting go from week to week. In 
this particular item, $85,000 represents the Record Office.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Where do we find the cost of the temporary clerks?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: They are still charged to Demobilization Vote. We have in the whole department 802 temporary clerks.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: How many in connection with the Record Office?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: How many will be required in the Record Office to carry on the work for years, as the minister says?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Seventy-four who have been classified as permanent and about 400 temporary, I think, probably for two years. Yon cannot make more than an estimate of that. I think, as I stated last night, the number will go down yearly, from fifty to sixty or possibly seventy-five of the present list being released this year. But after two or three years the number will be reduced rapidly because our records will be more or less complete.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the minister last year established a military body, a branch of the military service, to have charge of the records, or in any case that an establishment was given to the Records Branch?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I do not remember having ever mentioned the matter. Perhaps my predecessor did, but I am informed that if it was discussed-and it probably was- it was never carried out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Are these 74 permanent employees military men?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: A good many of them are returned soldiers; but they are on the civilian staff; they are not on the military staff of the department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Is it not a fact that there is some kind of a military establishment, calling for a colonel, so many majors, so many subalterns and so many non-commissioned officers in connection with the Record Office?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I understand that that was discussed at one time, but it was never carried out. Col. Armstrong, who is a member of the Permanent Force, is at the head of it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: His pay is charged to the Permanent Force appropriation?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Are there any other members of the Permanent Force in that branch?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I am informed that there is none.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: What is the total cost of the Record Office including members of the Permanent Force, temporary clerks and so on, at the present moment?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I have not the figures exactly, but I will endeavour to give an estimate in a moment or two.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I do not know whether the hon. member appreciates the importance of the Record Office. At one time an establishment of military staff clerks was considered. I think I can say, without fear of contradiction, that the Record Office is one of the most essential, economical and efficient organizations in the Government service to-day. There are in that Record Office, I think I am safe in saying, some
700,000	files giving a complete record of every officer, non-commissioned officer and man who enlisted in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, of the Government pensions, Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, Soldiers' Land Settlement, the various medals and rewards arising from time to time and the voluminous files that went with each man, as my hon. friend knows", from his enlistment station to the front in France. After the armistice those files gradually came back from France to the Record Office in England, from England to Canada, and they have been filed here in such a way as to form one of the most complete records in the Government service. It is most essential that the Record Office should be kept up to a high state of efficiency.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I agree with the view expressed by the former Minister of Militia and Defence that the Record Office has given us good service, and that it is absolutely essential to have a record office. This is certainly not one of the things instituted by the former Minister of Militia when his mind was inflamed by the war spirit, as his successor has just told us. The Record Office was absolutely necessary; we must have some place to which to apply for all the documents in connection with the soldiers who served overseas. There is a distinction between criticising the work of this office and finding out what it is costing us. If we need more for it, and it is shown that it is absolutely necessary to have more,
I would be the first to urge the Government to have some more money voted.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: An approximate estimate of the cost would be $600,000 for salaries and wages, and in addition to that there is rent, light, fuel, stationery.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Of which only $85,000 is charged against the Militia Department?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: $85,000 would be for permanent employees; the rest is paid out of the Demobilization Vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: What does the Separation Allowance and Assigned Pay Branch cost, and where is that to be found in the Estimates?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: In the Separation Allowance and Assigned Pay Branch there are fifty permanent employees and thirty temporary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: What do they cost in this vote?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Their salaries will
average about $1,200, so that would make $96,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: On this vote?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: No, fifty of them are on this vote; thirty of them are temporary and are paid out of Demobilization Vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: About $60,000 paid out of this vote?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Where will the remainder come from?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: In the Central Registry there are 43 permanent and 109 temporary. The average salary is the same-$1,200 each.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: That would make about $50,000 for the Central Registry. Who is in charge of the Separation Allowance Branch? Is he a military man or a civilian?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: A civilian, Mr. Cox, who has been there for a long time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Do any of those employed in the Separation Allowance Branch belong to the Permanent Force?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: No, I do not think there is a single individual.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Does the same thing apply to the Central Registry?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The total increase on
account of new branches over last year would be something like $85,000, the cost of the Record Office, $96,000; the cost of the Separation Allowance and Asigned Pay Branch, and about $50,000, the cost of the Central Registry.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Approximately, that
would be about right.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
So that the increase
should be roughly something like $225,000 owing to those three branches?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Those three branches would account for that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The increase would appear to be well over $400,000, or rather $350,000, after the deduction is made for the $50,000 which the minister struck off last night. Is there any other explanation to be given?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: There are 93 permanents in other branches than the three my hon. friend has enumerated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: 93 new permanents?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The total number is 259 in addition to the pre-war number. Today the total is 399.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: What are these other new permanents needed for?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: To perform the necessary work of the department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: What are they doing?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: My hon. friend must know that the work in every branch of the department has multiplied many times over what it was in pre-war days.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: As a direct result of the war. You have to continue to do the work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The war is over now, and we are looking after the effects of the war by means of the Central Registry and by means of our Record Office, which costs us $600,000. That is an important branch, and as I have already told the minister, we will give him all he needs for that branch. The Separation Allowance and Assigned Pay Branch has also to be kept on. I do not know just what it costs, but there is $96,000 in this vote, and Lord only knows what there is in the demobilization or war appropriation vote. The minister says there are 93 new permanents. I would like to know what they are doing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think it is simply a case of "right turn, dismiss?"

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: It^ should be, but evidently it is not. We have these three branches I have mentioned to look after the stragglers, but I want to know what these 93 new permanents are doing?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I can give my hon. friend the exact increases: Deputy Minister's office 1, Adjutant General 10, Central Registry 43, Printing, Stationery and Contingencies 7, Chief Accountant's office, which I did not mention before, 43, Director of Contract's Branch 20, Pay Service Branch 3, Separation Allowance and Assigned Pay 48, Chief of the General Staff, 1 Quartermaster General's Department 8, Engineer's Department 1, Survey's Department 8, Record Office 74. That makes a total increase of 267. Adding those to the pre-war employees gives a total of 399 permanents.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: That answers my question in a way, but then again it does not. I want to know why there has been this increase in these other branches, leaving aside as abnormal and non-permanent the Record Office, the Central Registry and the Separation Allowance and Assigned Pay Branch. Why are eight more employees required in the Survey's Branch, for instance?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
My hon. friend has
surely lost sight of this fact: In the year 1919, we had a staff of over 8,000 in the Militia Department; that was after the war. On the first of January last year we had cut that down to 5,200; that was the figure when I took charge of the department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The minister has done well.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
To-day the figure is down to 1,200. I cannot reduce any faster than I have done. When I do reduce I receive a good many complaints, not all coming from this side of the House. I am reducing the staff as fast as the work will permit. It is not a very pleasant task to have to reduce as fast as I have had to.
I have got it down to the point now where I must maintain a reasonable staff if the work of the department is to go on. Between now and the end of the year I expect to let out between 50 and 75 permanent employees, who have been made permanent for the reason I stated before.

The Civil Service Commission, under the statute, is authorized to give permanents a preference when let out and a vacancy occurs in some other department. If they were temporary, they would have no preference. In order to retain good men, we have had to do that. Some of these men are practically indispensible. Their knowledge is knowledge they have gained in the four years of the war. There are certain men we cannot let go without great loss to the service. I can assure my hon. friend that we have cut the staff down just as fast as circumstances would permit, and just as close as it can be cut, but instead of receiving thanks, I am sorry to say I am receiving anything but thanks in the letters which I am receiving, some anonymous, some signed, some from members, some from relatives and friends. It is not pleasant to reduce the staff as rapidly as I have had to, particularly in view of the unemployment situation in this country. I can assure my hon. friend we have had a good reason for retaining every man who has been retained, and that they are all performing service for the money received.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I heartily sympathize
with the minister. I know his soft heart must have been touched by the many appeals by members of Parliament. I can appreciate, too, his argument that members of the Civil Service would resign their positions if they were not made permanent. As to that, I put it to any hon. member of this House: Did he ever see any member of the Civil Service resign under any consideration? I think the experience of most of us would lead us to believe that the resignations that would occur through not being made permanent must be very few and far between. The other reason given by the minister, that it is necessary to make them permanent in order that they may obtain an entre into other branches of the service, is rather a peculiar one, too. We let them out of the Militia Department, but before doing so, we make sure they will find a home in some other department of the Government that might not be criticized so severely as the Militia Department. I cannot understand that line of argument at all.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: That is not correct, of course. The law of this country provides that a man who has been a permanent employee, and who has been let out, will be given the preference when a vacancy occurs in another department, over a man who was not permanent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The department says: We find, for some reason or other, that we want to get rid of him so we make him permanent in order that he may be transferred to some other department. That,
I think, is stating the case of the minister fairly.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
No, it is not; pardon
me for saying so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I think it is. However,
I do not want to be drawn into an argument on this point. I wanted to know why we had eight new men in the Survey Branch, and the minister held forth on his troubles and tribulations with regard to members of Parliament requesting him to retain certain members of the staff.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I did not get the minister's figures as to the number of men in the service when he took over the portfolio and the number now.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
There were 5,280 at
headquarters and in the 11 military districts when I took charge, and the number is now under 1,200 throughout Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
In what time has that
reduction been made?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: In fourteen months.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
What is the number of
males and females in the department, and of the males, how many are returned soldiers who served in the late war? How many temporaries are there also?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Of 269 additional
permanent appointments that are included in this item, 88 are returned soldiers. There are 60 other males, and 121 females.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The total number of
employees in the department, as given on pages 76 and 77, is 441; that is the number we are making provision for. It seems that the minister has reduced it by [DOT] 42, leaving a total of 399. How does that compare with the staff, say, in 1914, before the war?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: There were 117 permanent employees before the war.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: There has been an increase from 117 to 399?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
There have been 269
additional appointments.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I am asking for information and not criticising; but it seems to me that we should now be able to get back to something like pre-war conditions in this respect, and if 116, or 117 could do the



business before the war, why should 390 odd men be required now?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
In the course of three
or four years we shall no doubt be able to get back to pre-war conditions; but in the meantime we have a new department, the Record Office, which we never had before, and which will have to continue for five, six or seven years yet. That department employs the largest portion of the staff. The Central Registry, which employed two or three clerks before the war, became an enormous institution during the war, but it is now down to about forty-three; and the Assigned Pay and Separation Allowance Branch, which did not exist before 1914, was a huge institution during the war. It is gradually coming down, but it will be a year or two at least before any substantial reduction can be made there. Thousands upon thousands of disputed claims for separation allowance and for assigned pay are still pending and have to be dealt with by that department. That department is also used by the Soldiers' Settlement Board, by the Pensions Board, and by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, as are also the Central Registry and the Record Office. Without these three departments I doubt whether the Pensions Board or the other boards could function at all, because they would not have the information they require. The staff are kept hard at work, and they put in long hours. A reduction is being gradually made, and we let out a good many from week to week. The first of this month, a number were dispensed with, and I hope within a reasonable time to get down to pre-war conditions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
What about the Survey
Branch?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Here we have a lot of
topographers, etc., and I should like to get the information now.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
As the House is aware, the purpose of the Survey Branch is to make military surveys; it conducts the topographical survey of Canada. A very little portion of the map of Canada is done from year to year, and the work is not so much for the purpose of producing the map as it is for training military map draughtsmen. A very important part of the education of our militia and permanent force as

well is military draughtsmanship, and it is for that purpose that the Survey Branch is maintained in this department. I will give my hon. friend a resume of what is done and who are employed. Mr. Phelan is in full charge of all the instrumental control on which the maps are based. Major Browne is in full charge of all the topographic work, each being a supervisor of his section. Messrs. A. E. Attfield and A. Thomas are the more experienced topographers and have sub-charge of parties of junior topographers in the field. They also act as examiners of the field work. Messrs. Plamondon and Hay were not appointed until they had proved themselves to be specially efficient and reliable, after several years' service as seasonal employees. They both act as instrument men in charge of parties in the field; when required, also as topographers. Mr. Plamondon is also a trained air pilot and photographer. Though Mr. Cutts is classed as a military topographer, his duties are those of custodian of survey instruments and equipment; also of survey records. Mr. Cranston has had long experience in the Survey Division, in draughting and compiling maps. The other four gentlemen have been trained as lithographic map draughtsmen in commercial lithographic firms. The work done by these men is first class in every respect, whether on paper, stone or zinc. Owing to the increase of the work by reproduction of diagrams, the publication of the 1-inch maps has been retarded considerably. The printing plant could handle work from twice the number of draughtsmen, at least. Messrs. Smith, Crawford and Gow came from the printing establishment of the Geographical Section, General Staff, England, where they were trained as photographer, printer and lithographer, respectively. Messrs. Martell, Soutar and Carroll have received their training at the Survey Division. The three first men are experts in their different lines, and are deserving of every credit for the present efficient conditions of their departments. Of the two lithographic helpers, one acts as press helper and machine cleaner, etc., the other as stone polisher and plate grainer. J. Martell is assistant photographer, but acts as press feeder while printing is proceeding. Mr. Perkins is a specially skilful engraver, having been trained at the Ordnance Survey, England. His duties are to correct imperfections in etched copper plate originals; also to make corrections and additions to the old plates. He has

also engraved some very fine plates, direct. The map being the final test of the skill and efficiency of the whole staff, the Quebec 1-inch sheet, the last to he published, if examined in that light, will show a high state of efficiency at the present time. I can give my hon. friend a list of civilian employees of the Survey Division. I will first state the civilian employees on the permanent list before the war.
