maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Would it give the minister much work to find out what proportion of this vote is applied to the payment of salaries of parties connected with the demobilization?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: None of this particular item.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Perhaps I do not understand it aright but there is an asterisk referring the reader to the bottom of page 9 which says:
These votes include salaries and contingencies carried under the War Appropriation and Demobilization votes.	.
145i -
Would the minister explain what that means?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I am afraid I am encumbering Hansard with this explanation. Will my hon. friend excuse me if I put
it on record again.	,

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I am only a layman and therefore would like to have the explanation.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I think this is the fourth time I have given it. During the war only 120 of the present number of 399 represented in the item were carried under this vote and charged to the Militia Department. All the other employees of the department were war employees essentially, and they were charged to War Appropriation during the war, and to Demobilization after the armistice. Now it is thought that they should be charged against the department that is employing them. Three hundred and ninety-nine are included in the vote enumerated at page 8. They will in the future be charged directly to the Department of Militia, and not to War or Demobilization vote. There is an apparent increase but it is more apparent than real. Before the war there were 120 permanent employees. There have been during the war many thousands, of them, but we propose to make 399 permanent and to charge them directly to the Department of Militia.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: For demobilization?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: No, until we are able to reduce and get the staff down to something like normal conditions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Under what item are
the employees connected with demobilization paid?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: These employees we are now discussing in the Civil Government vote are yet largely engaged on demobilization work, but the temporary employees, and there are 800 of them, are paid out of the demobilization vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: May I ask the minister when he expects the demobilization will be over?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Strictly speaking it is over now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: What is the money for then?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The forces have been finally and completely demobilized both here and in Great Britain, save only those that ,are still patients in the Military

Hospital in Winnipeg. But the work consequent upon demobilization and upon the war itself will not, I think, he over for some years yet to come. As I said a few moments ago, it is quite possible that tlhe Record Office may have to continue with a considerable staff for five, six, seven or eight years yet to come. The others will more likely be reduced. It is my expectation that during the current year from fifty to seventy-five will be dropped. We will be able to drop that many from the permanent list, and at the same time each month we are reducing the temporary force also.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: If the demobilization is over why should the sum of $7,700,000 be asked for this year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: That question might be pertinent if you mean by demobilization simply the discharge of your army; but there are a tremendous number of outstanding accounts and adjustments yet to be dealt with, and claims are still coming in almost daily. There are claims in Great Britain-claims by shipping companies, claims by railroad companies; claims in this country and in London in respect of munition supplies-hardly a day passes that new claims do not come forward which have to be discussed, considered, and adjusted. So that this vote for demobilization, which last year was thirty-eight millions, we are glad this year to be able to reduce to seven millions, and our hope is that next year we may cut it down to one or two millions, or possibly wipe it out altogether. But so long as these-purely war claims -are outstanding it would be wrong to charge them against the annual vote of the Militia Department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: What investigation has the minister made as to the financial standing of these 120 females? I am advised by a person who was formerly a member of the stall of the Militia Department that a large number of these young ladies are daughters of men in affluent circumstances and do not need the positions, that they might very well be replaced by returned men. Has the minister made an investigation into all these circumstances so as to ascertain whether these young ladies should be kept on or not?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Of course we do not have the right to choose those whom we desire in every case because the Civil Service Commission makes the selection; we prepare the list but the commission makes the selection. I am not aware that there

is any foundation for the statement made by the member for West Peterborough, more than that, I believe the 120 female employees in question are of the ordinary type of a similar number of women employees in this or any other department. We try to select them by the rule of efficiency as nearly as we can, but in the first instance we try, as far as possible, to retain the services of returned soldiers. I may say that I have had many conferences with returned soldiers themselves with regard to the service, and I think I can say that the representatives of the soldier bodies are very well satisfied with what we have been able to do in the Militia Department in that respect.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I had the case in mind of a young woman whose husband was killed and who was a clerk in the British Admiralty office. She is unable to obtain a position, even of a temporary character, although I am told that there are many young women employed in the service in the city of Ottawa whose fathers are men of very considerable means and who do not need the positions at all and should not be there. I think the minister should make some representation to the Civil Service Commission, or introduce some amendment to the existing law, to provide that in the Department of Militia at least no persons except those who have the right by reason of war or other service, should be employed.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I think if the list is
examined in the Militia Department it will be found in every instance that the female employees are the representatives of families which have suffered in the war through the loss of brothers and fathers. I do not know anything about the wealth or affluence of these families, but their war sacrifice was taken into consideration. This list of female employees has been carefully con-my knowledge of the facts that there is sidered and examined, and I am sure from no substantial ground for the remarks of my hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Gordon), although there may be an odd case here and there open to criticism. Efficiency must count for something, but so far as possible we have considered first the returned soldier, and then the relatives of the returned soldier.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Does the Civil Service Commission consider the returned men and the families of those who rendered war service before making these appointments?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I understand they do.
It is legally their duty to give such classes the preference.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Shall
the item as amended carry?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
No, I have been waiting for some time to get an opening to follow up the discussion of Item No. 5 providing for salaries amounting to $643,751, the details of which are to be found on page 76 of the Estimates. This particular item consumed a lot of time last night, and the part that perhaps obtained the major portion of consideration was that which refers more particularly to the purchasing branch of the Department of Militia and Defence. It was shown by me last night, and it was admitted to a large extent by the minister, that either this purchasing branch . or the Purchasing Commission might be dispensed with. It seems to me that there is a duplication of service, not only in this department but also in some of the other departments. I find there are in this particular branch of the service twenty-two principal employees with, an aggregate salary of $40,980. In connection with them there is no doubt a staff of assistants representing another substantial amount for salaries? The minister, with his usual good nature, explained thoroughly to the committee both last night and to-night the various items in question. I find that this estimate calls for 441 employees. The minister has informed us that after this Estimate was prepared a decision was arrived at to strike off 42 of these employees. He also informed us that a certain number of those included in this Estimate will be retained in the service owing to war conditions. The Record Office claims 74 of these, the Separation and Assigned Pay 50, and the Central Registry Office 43, or a total of . 167. These deducted from the balance remaining after strik-
10 p.m. ing off the 42 leaves 232 employees. Now, if you deduct the employees in the Militia Department in 1914, numbering 117, that leaves still a balance of 115 unaccounted for. I would like the minister when answering to give an explanation as to the duties of these 115 employees.
My principal object in discussing this matter to-night is to focus attention more particularly on the purchasing staff. As I have stated, we have a large number of employees in this particular branch of the department, numbering 22 altogether. There are five purchasing agents with salaries of
$2,580, $2,220, $3,420, $2,280 and $1,680 respectively. The minister announced last night that the services of some of these men had been dispensed with, which would, of course, reduce the number employed in this particular kind of work. In addition to those discharged, a number of other employees are engaged in that class of work, including inspectors of hardware, leather products, textiles, mechanical and ordnance stores, assistant to the senior inspector of textile products, and so on. Their salaries aggregate $40,980. No doubt connected with this purchasing staff there are assistants of various kinds, such as stenographers, store clerks, file clerks, and so on. Probably the salaries of these would amount to no less than $9,020. That would make in round numbers a total of $50,000 for the purchasing section of the Militia Department. While we are spending all this money for purchasing supplies for the Department of Militia and Defence, I would remind the committee that we are also providing in these Estimates, under another heading, $80,000 odd for a purchasing commission. As I explained last night, either one or the other of these purchasing agencies should be dispensed with. If the purchasing agency of the department is not capable of performing the work for which it was originally organized its services should be dispensed with. If it is capable of performing the work, then I claim that the services of the purchasing commission should not be requisitioned to assist the agents whom we are paying so much money in connection with this department.
The minister informed us last night, and he has repeated the information this evening, that it is the intention during the near future to strike off a further number of employees from the staff, possibly fifty to seventy-five. Allowing a very low average of $1,000 each for the salaries of these employees, and putting their number at fifty, that represents an additional $50,000 in this Estimate that should not be required. I think the services of a further number of employees in the department might very well be dispensed with, seeing that it is the intention of the Government to curtail expenses as far as possible.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Alleged.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
We will give them credit for the full measure of their intention. They have announced time and again, and the minister has repeated it to us to-night, that it has been their desire in arranging the Estimates for the present year to cut

down the items to the last cent. Well, I think there are very many "last cents" still included, and I would suggest some of these "last cents" that might well be eliminated. I find in this list of employees a military contract engineer with a salary of $3,000, two topographical engineers whose combined salaries amount to $4,800, a map draftsman with a salary of $2,340, and two junior topographical engineers whose combined salaries amount to $3,840. It strikes me that a large part of this work might well be done by another department, say the Department of the Interior. That department has a complete staff of geographers, men expert in that kind of work. I think that saving, like charity, should begin at home, and if the Government wish to show their seriousness in the matter of saving they should eliminate all unnecessary duplication and centralize work of this kind in departments where it can be properly done. Why should the Department of Militia maintain expert geographers on their staff when there are men in the Department of the Interior who are thoroughly equipped to do the work and who probably have quite sufficient time to do it? Then, as I go through the list I find, 1 junior architect at $1,920. I may say that I do not know these gentlemen; personally I have nothing against them. I am merely discussing the matter as one who is really desirous of reducing the expenditure for this year. Then there is 1 junior engineer at $1,920. Surely this work could be performed by the Public Works Department. Then there are four senior map draughtsmen with salaries totalling $7,680; four military topographers, with salaries totalling $6,427; one senior photographer, $1,920; one photographer, $1,560; one assistant photographer $1,080. I do not know why the Militia Department requires the services of photographers. Are they to photograph the men on parade, or the officers, or the young ladies in the department? Just what kind of service are these photographers supposed to perform? Then there is another draughtsman at $1,200. It is not very much, but it is possibly all his services are worth. There is one copper plate map engraver at $2,040; two draughtsmen with salaries totalling $3,040; two lithographers, total $1,976; 2 pressmen and printers, $4,040; two duplicating machine operators, combined salaries, $2,220; one librarian, $2100; three secretaries to executive at $1,860 each, total $5,580. This makes a grand total for salaries in the list given of $58,-
683. The minister has told us that it is his intention during the current year to dispense with the services of between fifty and seventy-five employees. If we add to the amount that I have named, $58,683, the $50,000 for the purchasing staff and their assistants and $50,000 for say fifty employees that the minister proposes to dispense with during the current year, we get a total of $158,683. The total amount of the Estimate now under consideration is $643,751, almost three times the amount asked for last year. I do not think the minister has fully explained this large increase. He has told us that the staff was reduced from 5,000 a year ago to 2,500 the first of the year and now to 399. The minister himself has suggested a reduction in the Estimate of $57,320, leaving a balance of $586,431. Now, my desire is to assist the minister, and I suggest that he make a further reduction in this Estimate of $150,000, which is $8,683 less than the amount I have given as a possible reduction. I therefore beg to move, as an amendment to this item as amended, that a further sum of $150,000 be struck off the total amount of this vote, I am sure that this proposal will meet with the wishes of most hon. members. We all desire to cut down the Estimates as much as possible and we should show by our attitude in this regard that we are really sincere when we profess that we are desirous of carrying on the administration of the public affairs at the least possible cost to the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
In support of my hon. friend's motion, I have this to say: we have called the minister's attention to the fact that this vote under the head of Civil Government has been increased from $227,000 last year to $643,000 this year. In explanation of this large increase the minister tells us that we have been obliged owing to the war to add certain new branches and certain new services. He mentions three principal services. The Record Office costs about $685,000, of which $85,000 is included in this item. We have also a Pay and Allowance Branch which costs a large sum, of which $96,000 is included in this item, and we have a Central Registry, of which $60,000 is included in this item. Therefore, the minister's explanation covers really three branches, the expenditure in all amounting to something like $25,000, which, if we grant the minister's contentions to be true, would bring the item up to something like $500,000. As regards

the other $143,000 we have no explanation at all except that demobilization could not take place at once; that we could not simply "right turn and dismiss". There is no explanation why the different branches of the service which formerly existed must now have largely increased staffs. It seems to me that in the war appropriation and in the three special services mentioned, we have amply looked after the war and its consequences.
As my hon. friend (Mr. Pedlow) has pointed out, we have a duplication of purchasing services which might very well be done away with. We have a purchasing commission, appointed by the Government without sanction of Parliament, which is carrying on and doing all the purchasing of the Department of Militia and Defence as well as other departments. In spite of that, in this Estimate we have allowance made for different officials in connection with purchasing, and the sums to be voted for these amount to over $40,000. We have also a department of topography. The minister stated with perfect truth yesterday evening that topography was a most important branch of the military service; but if so, and it is important for soldiers to learn topography, why does the minister not employ soldiers in this branch so that they may learn topography and map reading and drawing instead of taking' in civilians to do the work? There is an important branch of the service called the Engineers. This engineering branch did remarkably good work during the war, and I do not see any justification for taking the work of engineering out of their hands and placing it in the hands of civil engineers. If any importance is to be attached to the work of military engineers, surely they ought to be allowed to practise at their profession in peace time.
Another item to which my attention was called by my hon. friend (Mr. Pedlow), although it is a small item, might very well be taken as an example of what might occur in other branches of the department. A salary of $2,100 is voted for a librarian. I do not know that there is a salary also for an assistant librarian. I am saying this subject to correction. But I notice in the Estimates that although the librarian obtains $2,100, we have never in previous years voted more than $1,000 for the purchase of books for this library, and this year we are voting $2,000, so that we pay a man more money for looking after the books than we do for the books themselves. If it is only a question of looking after the books, we could very easily dispense with the services of this librarian. We have a large number of soldiers otherwise employed in the department who could I am sure, give a good1 portion of their time to reading these books and taking care of the library without there being any necessity for a librarian. In support of my hon. friend (Mr. Pedlow), I urge upon the minister to reduce his Estimate by the sum named of $158,000. By so doing he will not injure the efficiency of his services, and he will at the same time be showing an example of economy in the department which should, I am sure, be the first to show examples of economy to the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: This item is the same as it was last year and in previous years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Will the minister give some explanation as to the allowances to officers of the active militia for command pay? How much is for drill instruction, how much for care of arms, how much for postage and so on?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: What are the trumpeter's duties? The minister does his own trumpeting pretty well.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I would have thought that a soldier of so much distinction as my hon. friend would have known that the allowance is not for the duties of a trumpeter. It is a special annual allowance of $3 to each trumpeter who has qualified at a permanent school and is found to be efficient at the annual training.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Why the $500 for fitting uniforms?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: There is an allowance of $1 apiece for fitting uniforms. As my hon. friend knows, all uniforms do not fit, and we try to adjust them as well as we can to the human body.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
There is an item for
special sized clothing under Clothing and

Necessaries. Why should not this $500 he brought under that item?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The Canadian Officers' Training Corps, which my hon. friend knows is in existence, gets an allowance of $1 for each member on his enrollment in that corps, under the Pay and Allowance Regulations.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Is that called capitation?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: No, although the capitation grant also pertains to the Officers' Training Corps. That is an annual grant of $5 to the Military Committee of the university for each member qualified as efficient. That is allowed under paragraph 63 of the Regulations.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Why does that not go into the Cadet Services? Is there a distinction between the Officers' Training Corps and the Cadet Services?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: We have tried as far as possible to keep the cadet training separate from the military training. The chief reason for separating them is to make the cadet service as far as possible a civil matter. The officers who take the Officers' Training course are usually above the age for cadet training.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Is there not an item for $20,000 for drill instruction?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: That was for care of arms.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: To whom is it paid?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: To officers commanding regiments of cavalry and infantry, and officers of other corps. It varies from $10 to $170 where there is no salaried caretaker, and from $5 to $100 where a paid caretaker is provided.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Where are these arms situated?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
In the armouries
throughout the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Are they regularly inspected?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Oh, yes, they are inspected by the officers of the district headquarters.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: To whom is command pay given?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: To the officers commanding the unit.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: In cases where the unit has not drilled, does the officer commanding the unit obtain this command pay, and care of arms pay also?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: No, he only gets a portion. Last year he was allowed 50 per cent of the pre-war basis, not full pay.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: If his regiment does not drill at all, why should he receive any command pay? Is there any reason?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The theory was that the various units had been pretty well knocked to pieces during the war, and they were all more or less in the process of re-organization. The commanding officers of the various units have devoted a tremendous amount of time to the work of re-organization, and while the unit in many instances was not up to the standard where it could drill and obtain a grant therefor, an allowance equal to 50 per cent of the pre-war basis was granted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Can the minister assure us that none of this money was granted to commanding officers who had no battalions or whose battalions did not drill? I do not know that we should be called upon to pay this command pay at all. When a man becomes a colonel of the militia, in the majority of cases he is only too glad to get the title and if it entails a little extra expense I do not think any commanding officer begrudges that $200 or $300.	The work which he does,
I am sure, does not amount to very much. He has to attend drills, it is true, and meetings of his battalion or regiment, but so no doubt have the subalterns and all the other officers, and the latter without obtaining the kudos and honour attached to the position of commanding officer. I know it is an old custom to give this command pay, but since the Government and the Minister of Militia have frequently stated that we should economize as much as possible, I do not see why we should not cut out this command pay altogether, particularly if the minister cannot state whether or not all the officers commanding actually had their regiments re-organized during the time for which they received this command pay.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I think there is a misunderstanding in the mind of the hon. gentleman in regard to this command pay. I can speak with authority of the city corps in particular. I think that at least 95 per

cent of the officers commanding the city corps never drew a cent of this command pay. I can speak positively of Ontario. I know that no commanding officer of any city corps in that province ever drew a cent of command pay for himself. Every dollar went back for the benefit of the militia. The officers, non-commissioned officers, and men refunded the small pittance they got from the annual training, and the officers commanding refunded their command pay. They used the money to maintain their regiments iri the efficient state in which the war found them. They did not draw a cent of this pay for themselves, but maintained their units on a sound foundation in order to rehabilitate them after the war. I know cases, particularly in Toronto, where the regimental funds were turned over to the expeditionary force units they raised. My home regiment turned its regimental funds, amounting to $22,000, over towards their expeditionary force units.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: What is the hon. gentleman's regiment?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The 48th Highlanders of Toronto. Then the 13th Royal Regiment of Hamilton, which I had the honour to command, contributed $13,000 to Canadian Expeditionary Force units. None of these officers in the last ten or fifteen years have drawn a cent of command pay. It was all turned in again to the regimental funds for the purpose of maintaining bands, paying a sergeant major, and the other numerous incidental expenses that a commanding officer is put to. The position entails a great demand on the commanding officer's purse as well as time. I think the efficient state of the militia units when the war broke out should convince everybody that the commanding officers were fully justified in using these grants for the benefit of their regiments.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I would be the last to criticise the ex-minister or any officers of the Militia Department who turn in their pay to the regimental funds, but that only goes to support my argument that we should not give this command pay at all. If the officers do not need this money, and can turn it in to the regimental fund, I do not see why the Government should be called upon to give it. Evidently, officers commanding regiments outside the cities of Ontario, and this is true, as I know of my own knowledge, of the cities of Quebec, pocket this money to be used for their own
purposes-legitimate purposes under the statute. If this grant is not necessary for the maintenance of the dignity of the officer commanding in city regiments situated in Toronto, Hamilton, Montreal, Quebec and Winnipeg, I do not see why we should make such a grant to keep up the dignity of the officers in the rural regiments.
I know, as no doubt many hon. gentlemen opposite know, that it is a very costly business to keep up a militia regiment in the city, and while I agree that the colonel who hands over his command pay to his regiment is worthy of commendation, still, on the other hand, that is no reason why the Government should make this grant. Either the Government can get enough money to support the militia or it should state openly that it is not able to do so. It has been said by the ex-minister, the member for Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn), that during the war a large number of these commanding officers kept up their battalions at great expense to themselves. I have no doubt about that, but I notice, in looking through the Auditor General's Report, that last year command pay was granted to a number of regiments, some of which certainly had not been drilled up to strength in the years 1918 and 1919, years for which command pay was given. I know nothing about any other district than that from which I come, but I find that the officers of certain regiments there, which never drilled during 1918 and 1919, drew command pay.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Name them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Every regiment in the Quebec military district apparently drew command pay, but I do not know that any of these regiments drilled during the war. There was a composite regiment composed of one or two. The point I make is that either the commanding officer of any of these regiments was, where he should have been, in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, in which case he drew his pay, or he was not in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and in that case he had no business to draw command pay for another regiment. If the system is to be continued, I think the item referring to command pay should be eliminated, and I therefore move that this item be decreased by $76,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: While I quite understand that my hon. friend is talking for political effect-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: -and I suppose it is good polities in some parts of the country to decry the militia-I think that no man who did distinguished service in the army should suggest for one moment that a cent of command pay was in any way misappropriated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: So far as I know, no commanding officer in any city or rural corps has ever drawn a cent of command pay, and it is unfortunate that we should have any insinuation-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I wish to correct my hon. and gallant friend. I made no insinuation whatever against any commanding officer; I said he took the money legally, and if my hon. friend construed my remarks as an insinuation, I am only too glad to withdraw any statement that lends itself to such a construction. I simply say that we should not have this item in our militia Estimates, hut I do not say that anybody takes any money unlawfully or illegally, or misappropriates it in any way.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Very well; if my hon. friend declares that he made no insinuation I am prepared to accept his statement. At the same time, I think we might very well seize this opportunity of paying a compliment to the militia men of the country, not only colonels and other officers, but men of the rank and file who from year to year gave every cent of pay to the general fund of their regiments. Everybody who knows anything about the militia knows that, and it would be a misfortune,
1 I think, if we should have even a doubt as to the patriotism of the militia, both before and throughout the war. My hon. friend must know that command pay is given for the purpose of reimbursing the commanding officer for certain necessary expenses-not social expenses-to which he is put in connection with his regiment; and it would be nothing short of a political disgrace in this country if this Parliament should cut down these Estimates, especially as we know that the department is always being assailed. My hon. friend the minister can never get the appropriations he requires for the purposes of a permanent militia, because, as I said a moment ago, it is considered good politics in some parts of the country to decry the militia.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I hope my hon. and gallant friend will not press this motion. I have been a member of the militia for twenty-eight years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Too long.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION

speechtext:
It is not often that I find myself in substantial agreement with my hon. friend from Simcoe as I do to-night. It would be a grave injustice to all the militia officers to make any insinuation to
the effect that they had misappropriated the public funds. I agree with the hon. gentleman in that respect, but I want him to help me to this extent:	Let him not allow
this House to get away with the impression, let him not attempt to impress the House with the notion that I have been insinuating that the colonels in the Canadian militia force have been misappropriating funds. If the hon. member wishes the idea to go out that such insinuations were made on the floor of this House he has but to make a speech such as he uttered a few moments ago. If the hon. member wishes to discuss the matter with me fairly and frankly he will do as he did in the beginning of his speech and admit that this money is not a payment to the colonels, or to the officers .commanding. He will admit that this money is voted simply as a species of grant made to help a militia battalion in its training. Well, if that be the case why in the world do we not call it a grant or pay the militia a sufficient amount of money. Then we would know, and the country as well, where we stand in this matter. We here vote a certain amount of money to every officer commanding presumably for his own use. He has a perfect right, under the law, to appropriate this money to his own use. If he does not wish to do so, if he wishes to give the money to his battalion, that is his affair; but my contention is that it is the duty of the Government to give this money frankly and openly and say "The Canadian Militia is not sufficiently paid; therefore, we want to make a grant for certain purposes. We want to make a grant for bands, and we want to make a grant 'for such and such a thing." Do not let us say we are giving it to the commanding officer if the commanding officer does not really receive it. I think the House and the country wish to know clearly where every cent of this militia money is going, and if we make it clear to the country that .this money is absolutely hecessary the better it will be for the militia itself and for the House as well.

Now I do not know any other way in which the vote could have been placed in the Estimates than the way in which it appears, so that it would have the right meaning and go to the right place, unless the commanding officer is mentioned. maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Will the minister explain the purpose of this item in view of the fact that we have so many soldiers in Canada that are already trained?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
This expense is for the purpose of training the soldiers who are coming on. I must take issue with my hon. friend in the suggestion contained in his statement that "we have so many soldiers in Canada." It is a suggestion made by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) last year when a similar vote was under [DOT] discussion. He seemed to take the ground that because we had perhaps as highly trained a force of experienced soldiers as any country possesses, that therefore we should not continue annual training; in other words, that this country should in future rely on the energy and bravery of the men who did so well for us in the last four or five years to protect us in the future. My view is that we had better get ready with another crop of men, and it is for the purpose of training the men now growing up and
[Mr. Currie. [
coming into our militia units that this $1,500,000 is asked. I must say that the amount is entirely inadequate for the purpose of training all the militia units that we would like to train. The amount for which a requisition was made in the first instance was $2,900,000. With the money asked for we will not be able to train the whole militia force this year. Last year we had no annual training except for city regiments, the reorganization not having sufficiently advanced for the holding of rural camps. Consequently there was a considerable saving in respect to this vote. In fact the total military expenditure last year was, I think, under $10,000,000, although the House voted $12,500,000. The main saving was on annual training, and the other large saving was on the arsenals at Quebec and Lindsay, which were closed for three or four months. This year, however, we propose to train the militia as far as we are able to with the money we are now asking Parliament to vote.	-
It will enable us to train a fairly representative proportion of the various units. In cavalry there will be twenty-three regiments at sixty-five per cent of strength. These will be required to train at local headquarters for a period of nine days, or in local camps in case the distance is short in order to save transportation. The horse allowance for the purpose of the cavalry units has to be estimated at $2 per day. In former years it was esimated at $1 a day, but from inquiry made in various parts of the country I think we will be well within the mark when we estimate the allowance at $2 per day for the current year. In artillery seventy-five batteries at eighty per cent of strength will train at local camps' for six days with horses. Then firing detachments will proceed to artillery practice camps for a four-day training. The old twelve days' training would be much better, I grant, than the six days' training proposed, but we have had to cut down the number of days in order to keep within the proposed expenditure of a million and a half dollars. However, when each battery trains a firing detachment will 11 p.m. be selected, and that detachment will be sent for fire training to some artillery practice camps for a period of four days. Infantry city corps, sixty-five battalions at sixty-five per cent strength will train at local headquarters for nine days, and not proceed to camps of instruction. Week-end musketry camps will be provided where required if money in the vote is available. Forty battalions of rural

corps will train at sixty-five per cent of strength, and twenty battalions will train on the same basis as the city corps themselves at local headquarters or at local camps for a period of nine days. Engineers, twelve field companies at sixty-five per cent strength will train at local headquarters or at local camps for a period of nine days. Signal corps: eleven companies at sixty-five per cent strength will train at local headquarters nine days. Cyclist corps: eight companies at sixty-five per cent strength will train at local headquarters nine days. Machine guns: twenty-five batteries at sixty-five per cent strength will train at local headquarters for nine days. Officers' training corps: twenty companies at sixty-five per cent strength will train at local headquarters nine days or at Ideal camps if feasible. Medical units will train at local headquarters at sixty-five per cent strength. Eight companies of army service corps will train at local headquarters or at local camps at sixty-five per cent strength.
That is all the training we are able to do on the vote which is now asked. If we trained all the available units to the full strength, my information is that about $2,900,000 would be required.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I would not oppose
this vote as strongly as I propose to do if the history of the last five or six years had not taught humanity that military preparations do not constitute any real defense of mankind. Of course that doctrine may have a somewhat strange sound to the ears of some military gentleman in this House, but I think if anybody will sit down
quietly and consider the events of the last five years he will be brought to the inevitable conclusion that the policy pursued in Europe of one country building up vast armaments against another, only resulted in the wiping out of a great proportion of the youth of all the beligerent nations in Europe-aye, not only the youth of those nations, but of the nations of other parts of the world who engaged in that war. Of course, militarists are never satisfied. Some of them wish to raise a fresh "crop" of young men for the next slaughter; and if the world in future depends, as it has depended in the past, on military preparation for security, war will come. Surely something has been learned during the last five years, surely we in Canada can lead the way in the reduction of military expenditure. There is no danger in the direction of our northern frontier, bounded practically by the north pole. Our neighbours to the south are bound to us by ties of language, custom, law, and relationship. There are almost as many Canadians and sons and daughters of Canadians in the United States as there are in Canada. Surely there is an opportunity for Canada to lead the way to reduction of armements and military expenditures. We are desperately hard up; we need every cent we can raise for the necessary expenses of the country. Surely this annual drill can be postponed for another year. Surely we should give the world a chance to devise some organization for the settlement of international disputes otherwise than by the blood of the young men. For, after all, it is the young men under twenty-five who fight wars and it is the older men of over forty-five who are in control of the policies that lead to war. I would invite the co-operation of all men in this House who are opposed to this sort of thing to vote down this resolution, and at least to postpone the annual drill until another year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I shall not accept the
invitation of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), because I think the theory that he announces is entirely wrong. We had not in Canada, any more than they had in Great Britain or in France, control over the military policy of Germany. If Great Britain had been as prepared as Lord Roberts would have had her prepared in 1914; had our great neighbour to the south been in a position to take an aggressive stand at the beginning of the war, the struggle would have lasted but a short time. I doubt very much whether there would have been a war at all; in any

event, tens of thousands of lives would have been saved. It is pacifists of the stamp of my hon. friend from Brome, men who go up and down the country preaching that sort of doctrine, who are responsible for the slaughter of millions of men that took place during the five or six years of the war. I am not desirous that money should be wasted on military preparations, but a country which is worth while is worth making preparations to defend; a country which shuts its eyes to the attitude and actions of other nations, folds its arms blissfully and says that it wants to have peace with everybody, will some day fall victim to the country which has kept itself prepared. My hon. friend might just as well say that the city of Ottawa in maintaining a police force was inviting people to go out on the streets and raise a row. There would be just as much sense in that argument as there is in the contention that we should not make some military preparation. I am not a military man; I am like my hon. friend from Renfrew (Mr. Ped-low), a very peaceable kind of man. But I repeat, that experience has taught us that it was the pacifists of Europe, of Great Britain, and of other countries, who were responsible more than anybody else for the great slaughter that took place during the war.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I notice that the next item is for cadet services, $450,000. The member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) contends that only those who share the views entertained by hon. members of this side are anxious to reduce the military expenditures. For his benefit, I would like to read the following statement sent to the New York World by the ex-Prime Minister, the member for King's (Sir Robert Borden), in a reply to a request from that journal, which is conducting a crusade for general disarmament on the part of Great Britain, the United States and Japan:
I sympathize most deeply and earnestly with every reasonable proposal for the reduction of armaments. Untold sacrifices endured in the great war will have been wholly in vain if the nations are still to compete in a mad struggle for supremacy in the power of destruction. The economic folly of such a policy is too manifest to be gainsaid. Is there not a sorrowful and bitter protest from millions on the verge of starvation in Europe and which must ring i4i the ears of every thoughtful person.
Continued competition in armaments assuredly brings the nations to ultimate disintegration of existing civilization, the foundations of which have already been rudely shaken. How can it be otherwise if to those who ask for bread civilization gives armaments. In the boundary between Canada and the United States, unfortified for more than a century, save by a common trust which has never been

violated, and in the intimate friendship which that just confidence has maintained and strengthened, we have given to humanity a lesson which ought never to be forgotten in the determination of this supreme question.
That is dated January 8, 1921, and it goes to show that the outstanding men of Canada are to-day unanimously of the opinion that in view of our great indebtedness and of the burdens which bear upon us-a condition which is common to all nations-we should lessen expenditures for military purposes. In the face of the problems that confront us; in view of our burdens of taxation, which may be increased in a few days when the Budget is brought down; in view of the extent to which people are trying to find ways and means of meeting their income tax liabilities, the returns for which, must ba in by the end of this month-for all these reasons, I feel justified in moving that item No. 89 be reduced by $750,000.
Amendment (Mr. McCoig) negatived: Yeas, 47; nays, 72.
