maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: We should like to have some particulars concerning this item.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The amount voted last year was $390,000, and the amount asked this year is $450,000, or an increase of $60,000. But even for the pre-war year of 1913-14, there was an expenditure on this vote of $392,000, so that there is not a very great increase over that pre-war year.
The general purpose of the vote is for the cadet services in Canada. Under the provisions of section 64 of the Militia Act cadet corps may be of three classes in Canada: First, those composed of pupils at colleges and schools controlled by the government of the province in which they are situated; second, those composed of pupils at colleges and schools not under government control, and third, those composed of lads who, with the permission of their parents or guardians, prefer to join a corps unconnected with any educational establishment. We have the three classes of cadet corps in Canada now.
It is proposed to provide for the instruction of 85,000 cadets, there being almost that number at the present time enrolled in Canada. The cost is two dollars each for the first fifty and one dollar each for those in excess of fifty in each company or corps under the same instructor, and for uni-

forms for 48,000 cadets, an allowance of $1.25 per cadet. In 1914, 11,408 cadets were trained for six days. During the summer of 1921, it is proposed to train 8,000 for eight days. There will thus be 3,000 fewer cadets trained than in the year before the war, but there will be two days' longer training. For general training in school and out of camp, the expenditure proposed is $321,050; for the cadet camp for 1921, the expenditure proposed is $128,260, making a total expenditure of $449,310.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Does the minister not think that we could worry along with the same number of cadets that we trained last year at a cost of $390,000, seeing that we have to pay about $25,000,000 or $30,000,000 on the deficit on our Canadian National railways more this year than last year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I am rather surprised at the suggestion of my hon. friend, because the demand for increased cadet training comes from the city of Montreal and particularly in regard to the schools. The figure of enrolment of cadets has gone up very largely; it is now up to 84,000, and if the Protestant schools of Montreal adopt the system, as it is expected they will adopt it, there will be another very , large increase. I do not think we could ask for a smaller contingent than 8,000 at the annual camp. The rest of the cadets receive training at the schools or in their classes. For the purpose of the camp we are asking for 8,000 cadets, or 3,000 less than the year before the war.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The minister will admit that the training of lads in these public schools must be considered as more or less of a luxury, if I may so term it. Could not this cost be reduced^to the same amount as last year? As I have just pointed out, we need this money much more than we did last year. There ought to be some paring in some of the departments. The minister seems to adopt a hard and fast rule; he is riding with top-boots and spurs; he insists upon having the whole of this amount which is mentioned in the Estimates, and he is not agreeable in cutting down any sums whatever. It is patent, I think, to every hon. member in this chamber that the training of cadets is not an essential feature in the life of the country at the present time, and if there is any place where we could cut down expenditure, it ought to be in these matters. The
minister says that he is surprised that I should object to this, seeing that the city of Montreal is one of the chief sinners in demanding this increase.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I did not say "sinners."

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I am not responsible for the conscience of every citizen in Montreal, which is a large city of nearly 800,000 people. I suppose the citizens of Montreal, being rather astute people, finding that this money is so easily obtainable, do not see why they should not get a share of it while the getting is good. This is certainly an item which we on this side are strongly objecting to, and I would move that the amount be reduced to $390,000, the same as last year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I regret exceedingly that the hon. member seeks to reduce this very important vote. My great regret is that the appropriation is not double this amount, because the inauguration of the cadet service in Canada was of the greatest benefit to this country. The high school and public school cadet corps inculcate into the youth of this country patriotism, discipline, and the benefits of physical development. The record of the cadets in the war is a record of which any country ought to be proud. I think I am safe in saying that at least 50,000 cadets who went through training in the schools, enlisted in the Canadian Expeditibnary Force. As I said before, the physical development, the discipline and the inculcation of patriotism in the youth of this country are worth millions of dollars to Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The hon. member who has just resumed his seat has made the statement that military training inculcates patriotism in the youth of this country. Well, it is patriotism at some other person's expense. If the parents of these boys are so patriotic, surely they ought to pay $1.50 or $2 in order to see that patriotism is fostered and inculcated. Any person who wants the other fellow to pay for his education in patriotism is a very poor sort of patriot.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I have in mind that some years ago a previous Minister of Militia announced to the House that he had received a grant from some person, I am not sure just who, for this purpose. Is there a special endowment grant for this purpose?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
It is the fund created by Lord Strathcona. It is invested and

produces $20,000 a year, which is administered under a special trust. The whole income from the fund is devoted to the training of cadets, and is divided among the various provinces of Canada. A meeting of the trust was held within the last six weeks, and I think all the provincial educational institutions were represented at the meeting. The money was divided on that occasion on a proportionate basis as between the provinces.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: And this vote is in relation to that grant?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: We have listened to arguments, especially from military men, as to the necessity for military training, and the virtues it develops. I think it would be well for us to review the past for a moment or two, and we need go no further back" than the last war, to see whether military training is valuable or not. This country, previous to the war, had been spending annually large sums of money on military training. When the war broke out, quite a large percentage of the men on whom the country's money had been spent for annual drill did not go to the front at all, for some reason or other. There is no man in this House or outside who has more respect than I have for the man, whether he had previous military training or not, who went to the front and defended our country in her hour of need, but I wish to point out some facts which I think should be a guide to us in deciding whether or not it is really in the best interests of the country that every man should receive a military training. I have said that a large percentage of those who had had military training previous to the war did not enlist, and of those who had received military training and did enlist many went over to the other side as majors and colonels and officers of other rank. When they got over to England they found that there was no place for them in their respective ranks, and as they did not wish to step down and become a private, they remained in England and did not do the fighting.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: How many?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The great percentage of the men who went over to France and did the fighting had never had military training at all until they enlisted, and they made just as good soldiers and defended their country just as well as the men who had had military training. What about the great number of men who had had mili-

tary training in this country and who went over to England as colonels, generals, majors, and everything else, spent their time in England and never saw a battle? Was military training valuable in their case? Is it wise in the face of these facts that every man should receive a military training from his youth up, so that when war comes he will be able to say: "I am a colonel, and if I get an appointment as a colonel, I will fight, but if I don't, I won't." For that is what happened. Our experience in the last war was that the men who had had no military training at all were just as willing to serve their country as the men who had had training. In view of these facts, and the heavy financial strain that this country is under, I would plead with the Minister of Militia to cut down every dollar of expenditure he possibly can in all directions. We have no money to spare. I really do not know that this country is in such a desperate haste for money to be spent for military purposes for some years to come. I think the war we have just gone through has been a lesson to most nations, and that they will avoid war as far as possible in future. Let us commence by avoiding this military expenditure.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I should like to answer a statement made by the ex-Minister of Militia (Mr. Mewburn). I am of the opinion that there is a war party in Canada, and if the people of this country were here to-night and could see the hon. gentlemen who are supporting these items they would find out who belong to the war party. On March 31 of last year I placed myself on record as being opposed to the spirit of militarism, and I have not changed my ideas on that subject in any respect since then. I referred last year to the instance in 1870, when militaristic Germany defeated militaristic France. I can imagine the same sort of thing carried to an extreme by the war party in this country. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Militia gives the credit to the cadet training for all the virtues these youths possess after having undergone a course of training. It is not entitled to the credit. "Theirs not to reason why, theirs but to do and die." It is simply a case of subordinating the will of the boy who is growing into manhood to the will of one they call a superior. They say this training makes the boy strong and gives him great self-control. That is the reason, I suppose, why we have

the very common saying about a person swearing like a trooper.
I would ask the minister if this item has anything to do with the purpose indicated in the statement that was made by a brigadier general of Military District No. 12, to the effect that a military course would he given in the provincial university of Saskatchewan this year, which would embrace all the engagements in the war, attack, defence, and so on. Is a similar course to be given in the other provincial universities? I have received protests from the people because of the institution of this course, and I might also say that I have received protests in connection with the $500,000 endowment fund created by Lord Strathcona for military training in the public schools. There are a great number of people who object to their children receiving military training at school. While it is claimed it is optional, if the child in his innocence does not inform his parent it may be taken for granted that the parents consent, and the boy will be trained. When it is found out, the parents disapprove. I want to know if it is the policy of this country to start giving the boy military training when he is at school, and to follow that up through the universities. If so, I can imagine the time when we shall have expenditures similar to those in the United States. I should like to put certain figures on Hansard, and if people will read the few remarks I make, and pay particular attention to the facts I cite-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Well, let me tell hon. gentlemen opposite that the feeling is rampant in this country that the military spirit is too much in evidence. Now, the following are the United States appropriations for the year 1920:
Past Wars	$3,855,482,585
Future Wars	 2,424,138,677
Civil Departments	 181,087,225
Public Works	 168,303,557
Education and	Science....	57,093,661

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: From what source is the hon. member quoting in regard to the United States?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I am quoting from the United States trade returns.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: From the trade returns?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The figures are taken from the report of the United States Auditor General.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Well, they are very different from the figures furnished us.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: They are totally different from the way you have them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: If hon. gentlemen opposite want the percentages, I will give them.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: No; I do not want them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: These are the percentages: For public works, three per cent; for education and science, one per cent; for civil departments, three per cent, for past wars, 68 per cent, and for future wars, 25 per cent. Compare these expenditures for civil government, for public works, and for education and science, with the tremendous appropriations for war, and you will see what the upkeep of military establishments means. There are people in this country who would lead Canada into the same condition. Last year I rose and protested against the continuance of this military idea, and I repeat that protest on this occasion. I deplore the fact that there are men in this country who see fit to prolong an extensive military establishment, and hon. members will find that the words uttered on this side to-night in protest against this extraordinary and inordinate expenditure will be echoed by the people at the first opportunity. I am sure of this.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Let me reply to some observations made by the member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea). The first statement he made was that there was no use in training a militia because the experience of the last war had shown that militia men did not take part in the war. I do not know for what part of the country he speaks, but so far as the part of the country from which I come, and other parts with which I am familiar, are concerned, I will say that every known militia man got into the war as soon as he could. The hon. member further said that the nonsoldier, the man who had not been trained, had done as well as the soldier who had undergone training. One sometimes hears this statement outside, and there could be no greater fallacy. The fact of the matter is that in the first division the greater proportion of the non-commissioned officers and officers were men who had seen lengthy service in the Canadian militia, and who owed their entire adaptability to the training they had received in the militia. Subsequently, as further divisions were



created, the men who had received their training in the militia, profiting by the additional experience gained in the war, rose to the command of all the higher formations, and throughout the war, not only in our service, but in every other service, it was absolutely demonstrated that the man who had received the most training was the best man. He was the man who was trusted both by those under him and by his superiors; and to suggest now that training is of no value is not only fallacious, but is also dangerous and detrimental to the best interests of this country, which has relied in the past, as it will probably do in the future, upon trained men. The member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould), like many others who think as he does, asks the question: where is the enemy? I took the trouble the other day to read the debates in this House on these very Estimates in 1914, in 1899, and in 1884, and it is interesting to find, although it is regrettable, that the House has always contained a certain number of men who were prepared to criticise these Estimates with no greater intelligence than these gentlemen display.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Take it back.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Some exception has
been taken to the proposal for cadet training, and objection has been offered particularly to the idea put forward by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn) that this training inculcates sentiments of patriotism in the young men of the country. The hon. gentleman from Assiniboia deprecated the inculcation into the minds of these young men of the military spirit. Well, I know of no quality of greater value to the country in time of need than the military spirit. But for a high military spirit in this country we could not have raised the army we did, and could not have had the success we had. I cannot for the life of me understand the outlook of a man who deprecates the spirit that impels men to the front in time of danger and inspires them with the belief that they can do no greater service to the state than to lay down their lives for it; and I am forced to say that if this country had contained any considerable number of people holding the views of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) and the hon. member for Assiniboia, Canada would have curled its tail between its legs and crawled under cover.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
At the
risk of being termed an ignoramus by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Griesbach)-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: He knows it all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I must protest against what I might term, if it were not perhaps unparliamentary, his impudent suggestion in his closing remarks; and certainly 1 utterly disagree with him on the question of the value of militarism and the military spirit. I know quite a number of boys who went to the front, having been closely associated with many of them, and I can say that the vast majority of the young men who went to the war when men were most needed, had no military training, although they were just as good as any man who ever fought in the trenches.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Excuse me-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Order, order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: May I say-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Order, order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I want to ask my hon. friend if he knows of any soldiers that fought in the front line trench in France that did not have six months training?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I know
of soldiers who went to the front who had not the slightest training until the war came on.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: They had six months training.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
They
trained during the war and not before it, and they were just as good soldiers as the fellows that had been trained. I think my hon. friend made a reflection on these men because they went at the very time they were most needed and they were the most patriotic. They were not men imbued with the military spirit; they were utterly devoid of that spirit. They did not want anything of the kind, they hated the idea -of going to war, hut they believed it was their duty to go and they went. These are the men who saved the country, these are the men who saved the situation, not our militarists. I do not wish to oppose any reasonable expenditure for military purposes, and I would not have risen had it not been for the strange remarks which my hon. friend made. I think those remarks were utterly uncalled for and that my hon friend should apologize for making them. Now let me say this: I have stated

that I do not wish to oppose any reasonable expenditure for military purposes. I think this is a time when instead of increasing military expenditure we should take a military holiday and cut out military expenditure as far as we can. Just at the present time there does not seem to be any great necessity for it to my mind. In my boyhood days I underwent military training too, and I believe there was more need for it then than there is now; there was more chance of war then than there is at present. I like to see the boys taking a military training when they feel like it, but I see no reason-and no legitimate excuse has yet been given that I have heard -why we should increase this expenditure for cadets. The suggestion was. I think, to cut it down. I see no reason why we should not do so. I see no reason why at the present time, with the present financial situation as it is, we should not cut down the military expenditure, at least for a year or two. I would ask the Minister of Militia to try and take the suggestion into his consideration. I believe that in some particulars he has been cutting down considerably. I believe he has been trying to cut military expenditures down hut I think he has not gone far enough. He has not gone as far as the people of the country think he should go, and as far as we have a right to expect him to go.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle is trying to take a reasonable view of the situation and I want to show him that I have been reasonable also. I think one good way of showing that is to put Canada side by side with almost all the other civilized countries.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Well, I do not know how you can form a fair estimate if you do not make a comparison with some other country. We must compare ourselves with the Australians who are very nearly in our situation, with the New Zealanders who are somewhat in our situation, with our friends in the United States-a nation of intelligence-and with the European countries with whom we were allied. They have some intelligence and so has the Mother Country. Now if we are below any of the countries I have enumerated in our proposed military, naval and air expenditure do not hon. members think I have established the fact that we have been fairly reasonable? Do hon. members know what we propose to expend this year in Canada? This is the proposal: For this year the 1461
military expenditure proposed in these Estimates is $11,890,000, the naval expenditure $3,726,980 and the air expenditure, including civil aviation, $1,625,000 making a total for defence purposes, including civil aviation, of $17,241,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
What about the navy?
Is the navy included?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I have included it. I am told that my figures for the naval expenditure include provision for wireless operations and the like. The total is seventeen and a quarter millions in round numbers or $2.15 per head for the people of this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Too much.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Now go to Australia. There the average is $6.13 per head. Go to New Zealand and the average is $5.82 per head.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Too much.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Go to Great Britain and the amount there is $22.36 per head, and to the United States where it is $13.13.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: It is all very well for hon. members to say "No" but is not the comparison I make a fair one? If it is not, with what country am I to make a comparison.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Have we the money?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Let me mention these facts: Last year we proposed twelve and a half million dollars and the House voted it. We spent between nine and a half and ten millions. I have cut that down under the Estimates of this year by $643,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Continue it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Have my hon. friends heard anybody pay me a compliment for doing so? I have not heard any myself. As I say, we have cut the Estimates this year by $643,000

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Do some more cutting.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: -without a word of approval being heard from hon. gentlemen opposite. I say also that in comparison with all the civilized countries I have enumerated our expenditure for this purpose is the lowest by dollars, and dollars and dollars.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Perhaps we are not
civilized.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: We have cut the expenditure right down to the lowest margin of safety and anybody who is satisfied with a reasonable expenditure should, I think, support the modest programme we put forward on this occasion. My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle knows as well as I do that the cost of maintaining the military organization to-day is just double what it used to be. Our wages are increased by ninety to one hundred per cent for all ranks. Our clothing is over one hundred per cent dearer than it was in pre-war days. Our food allowance is over one hundred per cent greater. The cost of transportation is seventy to eighty per cent dearer. Take my $11,900,000 proposal to-day and apply the prices on the basis of the value of money as it existed in 1905 or 1906 and we are down to an actual expenditure of five or six millions1-we are back to what we spent in the early days of Sir Frederick Borden's regime. Surely that is a reasonable proposal which my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle can support.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I do not know what the military expenditure was in the years 1906 and other years.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
It was' between five and six million dollars. I will give my hon. friend the exact figures because I have them here. For 1907-08 the expenditure was $5,868,000, and comparing the value of the dollar then and the purchasing power of the dollar now the expenditure proposed is just about $6,000,000 at the present time. For 1908-09 the expenditure was $6,749,000; for 1909-10, $6,109,000; for 1910-11, $7,026,000; for 1911-12, $8,199,000; for 1912-13, $9,376,000; for 1913-14, $11,-
278,000.	Now I think with these figures, and the statement I have made, my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle-who I know is inclined to be reasonable in these matters -will conclude that this is a reasonable proposal and one that ought to be supported.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
If my hon. friend has not been congratulated I will congratulate him on having made the reduction he has. I am sorry that I cannot congratulate him to a much further extent because I do not think his reasoning is at all good. He compares us with other nations and says the comparison is a fair one. As a matter of fact we are not in the same position as any of these nations. My hon. friend knows very well that the position in Australia and New Zealand is very different from what it is here. People

in Australia and New Zealand are frightened of Japan. What are we frightened of? Are we afraid of the United States?	.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Yes, and so is Japan.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
If we are, I do not
think any militia we raise will save us.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
That is not a very
patriotic boast.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: What about the European nations? What is the use of comparing us with them?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I did not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Will you undertake
to say that we are establishing a militia to protect us from our neighbours? That is what the people of Europe are doing to-day. Now, let me say to my hon. friend with regard to the comparative expenditure in 1905 and 1906, when it was about half what it is now, and when it is true the dollar was worth about double its present value, I quite agree that practically the expenditure was roughly the same. But the situation to-day is different. At that time the finances of the country were booming, we had lots of money to spend; we have not now. The Government is continually telling us that we must curtail our expenditure. People are clamouring for expenditure in my part of the country. When I go to the Minister of Public Works I say to him, "I understand the Minister of Finance is close, but I must lay this proposal before you." That is all I dare do. The Government say that this or that thing should be done, but we cannot do it, I think the Government are perfectly justified in assuming that attitude, and I am prepared to back them up in everything tending towards retrenchment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Was not the expenditure in 1906 a larger percentage of the revenue of that year than this expenditure is of (the revenue of this year?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I agree, but surely
my hon. friend knows that that is not a fair comparison. What is the expenditure largely caused by? By the aftermath of .the war, is it not?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I was asking if the
expenditure in 1906 was not a larger percentage of the revenue of that year than this expenditure is of the revenue this year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Quite true, but my
hon. friend is drawing a herring across

the path. He knows that the greater part of the revenue now raised is for paying the debts incurred by the war. Why does not my hon. friend mention that fact if he wants to be fair? At this time I see no special occasion for either military or naval expenditure. Before the war we always had the fear of Germany hanging over us, and we did recognize that there was (some danger of a great European war. But that is a thing of the past. The great need now is not to prepare for war, but to save every cent we can in order to get our country in the financial position it should be. Therefore, while I have to congratulate my hon. friend the minister in what reductions he has made, I wish he would go further and entitle himself to still greater congratulation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise for the purpose of very briefly replying to some observations made on the opposite side of the House which to a certain extent have been directed at me. I do not propose to continue the discussion with any heat, because the subject matter is of such outstanding importance that in comparison any individual member's personality fades into utter insignificance. The member for Frontenac accused pacifists-and I am proud to call myself one-of being the cause of the late war. The people who wanted to be peaceful, according to the member for Frontenac, are those responsible for the war. If they had only been prepared to put on a more ag-12 m. gressive front the war would have been avoided. Might I tell him that I interpret the history of the last few years very differently indeed. It seems to me that the fundamental causes of the war were the conflicting interests of European imperialism, that the greatest sinner in that respect was Germany, but that no great nation is free from blame. And I would remind him and other hon. members that as great an authority as Lloyd George himself said that the civilized nations of Europe had more or less slipped into the war. I would beg hon. members to read the White Paper issued by the British Government shortly after the war started, and I believe if they calmly consider the story disclosed in those telegrams and letters, when one chancellory was frantically telegraphing to another, when one ambassador was in hourly communication with other ambassadors and with his home office, they will realize that great agencies of destruction were put in motion, and once
in motion those at the head of affairs could no longer control them.
The member for West Edmonton (Mr. Griesbaeh) referred in language, which I doubt was parliamentary, to the fact that if there had been many people in this country like the member for Assiniboia and myself at the beginning of the war Canada would have curled its tail between its legs and taken refuge under the barn. Might I tell him and other hon. members that, what rallied the great British people in support of the cause of the Allies, and what rallied the Canadian people to that cause was the belief that they were fighting against militarism, that they were fighting against that spirit which has been so aptly demonstrated by the member for West Edmonton himself to-night. What raised our Canadian army? I did not go to the war, I did not think it my duty, but a great number of my friends did, and many of them will never come back. A great number of those men went, not because they were imbued with the military spirit, but because they hated it, because they believed they were fighting a war to end war; and if they look down from the place of their last reward now it must be with sad hearts to see how little this war has ended war.
Of all controllers of foreign policy the militarists are the most dangerous. In Europe before the war who was really in control of foreign policy but men like Von Tirpitz, who imposed his will upon Germany, and great soldiers in other lands who imposed their will upon their governments. When a war was on it was natural enough that the soldier would dominate policy. Well, he dominated policy in Europe for five years, and where is Europe to-day as a result of militarism? I do not propose to attribute the blame for the war to this or that nation, I believe, as I have said before, that the greatest sinner was the late Empire of Germany, but I believe that no militaristic nation can escape some measure of blame. But to what pass have the soldiers brought the world? To this pass, that Europe, probably the most highly civilized part of the known world, is to-day on the verge of bankruptcy, that this generation of young men has been largely wiped out, that children born in the warring countries during the war have died in infancy or survived only to drag out a miserable existence by reason of the fact that their health had been undermined. That is the result of allowing soldiers to control policy. You

cannot blame them. No matter how good their intentions may be, if their minds and hearts are set on organizing machines for destroying their fellowmen, it is no wonder that they want to see those machines in action sometime. I have been shocked, as a great many hon. members have been, to hear the light references made by some people to the "next war." If there has been a lie which has deluded humanity for generations-aye, for centuries-it has been that in time of peace we must prepare for war. I say with all the conviction of which I am capable that if you prepare for war you will have war, and it is about time that the world and humanity tried to prepare for peace. If to take that view is to lack intelligence, I must plead guilty to the charge. If belief in that is to be compared to the action of a cur-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: If the hon. member believes that to prepare for war produces war, does he believe also the converse, that by not preparing for war you escape war?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I believe that, in very large measure. I believe that if you prepare for peace you have far more chance of having peace than if you prepare for war.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I would point out that we
must be doing that, because the minister has reduced the total Estimates for this year by $640,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I am quite willing to give him thanks for that reduction. It is as if we asked him for a loaf and he handed us a wafer, but we ought to be thankful that he has gone that far. I put it to hon. members: Is it wise to refuse the request made from this side?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Well, perhaps those
who are noisiest on the other side do not represent the real feelings of the Canadian people. My belief is that when we come to vote on this item there will be many men on the other side who would, if thew felt themselves free from the party trammels which bind them, be only too happy to vote with us.
Mr. McGIBBON Muskoka) : It is quite evident that the hon. member for Brome and many others have forgotten the history of the last few years. As I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Brome I felt that I was transported back to the year 1913 and was listening again to the speeches
TMr. McMaster.l
delivered from the opposite side on that occasion. We all remember the arguments advanced then to the effect that there was no danger; that the horizon was clear- arguments advanced, Sir, up to within sixty days prior to the outbreak of the war. Hon. gentlemen are repeating their tactics of 1914. What was the condition of that year? Germany was able within fourteen days after the declaration of war to put 225 trained divisions in the field. France, the next best prepared, could put only 75; Russia 50, and Great Britain only 6. Is there a sane man here to-night who would say that had Britain been able to put 60 or 70 fully equipped divisions into the field at that time, as she was later, war would have broken out? If there is, let him refer to history. Let him read the messages that came from the President of France, not to the Government of England but to the King of England himself. Let him read these in the light of history and see whether the whole war would not have been averted and the great list of casualties resulting from the war avoided if England had been prepared as I suggest. We have been told tonight that Canada produced an army which, although untrained, was equal to any in the world. England fought her first severe battle September 25, 1915. Of course there were engagements before that, but the first battle of great magnitude was fought on that day. And why? Because it took them all that time to get ready-and they were not ready then. Every man knows who had anything to do with the war that England was not ready until the following year, 1916. The hon. member for Brome askr where Europe is to-day. I ask him where the British Empire would be to-day had it not been for the trained troops of France who stood in the gaps in France and Flanders while the British Empire was getting ready. That is the question that we should take into consideration. As to putting green troops into the trenches, you could not make a more preposterous proposition to any army in the world. Those of us who were over there saw untrained troops come in occasionally because it was necessary, but only with dire results not only to themselves but to the rest of the army. We should get back to some sanity on this question. Canada, like every country, must be prepared to defend herself; and we must train new men-you cannot expect these old soldiers to be going on year after year and fighting the battles of the country while others sit down and pass their time in

peace and ease. Besides, the great bulk of them feel that they have done their duty.
I say that when hon. gentlemen challenge the passing of items involving a few paltry dollars to prepare for the protection of this country in case of emergency they are employing the same tactics, adopting the same short-sighted policy, using the same silly, incompetent arguments which characterized their utterances oh this subject before the great conflict broke out in 1914.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I would like to know what present or immediate danger the minister referred to when he said that we had cut down the Estimates to the lowest margin of safety. Was it Japan? Was it the United States? Was it any country? Well, if the minister does not wish to explain, I can continue for a little while. Apparently he is not clear in his own mind from whom we may apprehend the danger. If we are proposing this large expenditure for the purpose of developing a military spirit- and that seems to be the only reason so far given-then it is my view that we should cut out the military expenditure altogether. In that respect, I share the view of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), that if you teach people the use of deadly weapons, if you bring them to glorify war and the making of war, you will inspire them with a spirit which will bring them to use those weapons and to believe in war as a settlement of their difficulties. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Brome, it has been the experience of the past five years that the more militarism is encouraged in the country, the more we may expect at some time or another to enter into a deadly conflict. We are, it is true, spending about the same amount as we were spending previously to the war. The minister has pointed out that we are spending something like $12,000,000, or rather really for military and defence purposes, $17,000,000. That sum of $17,000,000 is devoted to defence purposes only; but the minister refuses to tell us what we are defending against, what enemy we have in view, and I cannot for the life of me see any on the present horizon. We have this amount of $17,000,000 for no real immediate danger, and the minister wishes us to vote it because it is no greater than the amount voted in 1913. I would call the minister's attention to the fact that, in 1913, a large number of people in Canada believed that there was an immediate danger that war was about to break out owing to the very fact that European nations were arming
and preparing for war at some time or another, so that there might have been an excuse at that time for military preparations. Personally, I am inclined to share the view of the leader of the Opposition of 1909, the ex-Prime Minister of this country, the hon. member for King's, (Sir Robert Borden) who, in 1909, stated that the $6,000,000 appropriation for militia purposes should be cut in half. I am inclined to share that view, and I would have been inclined to share that view in 1909; but if the militia vote should have been cut in half in 1909, when we had a real danger to face, surely we should have no expenditure at all when in the last war we have done away with the greatest enemy whom we would have had to face, and with the only enemy whom we could possibly be called upon to face.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: As regards expenditures in the United States, what amount is for military purposes, as apart from naval expenditure?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
These are the figures
of the last Congress: Military, $639,275,503; naval, $644,515,731; air, $95,000,000; total, $1,378,791,234. This is the expenditure of the national government for military, naval and air purposes; but in addition to this, there is a very heavy expenditure by the states themselves on the National Guards which are maintained in each state. The National Guard expenditure, by the states, is not included in the items which I have given.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Clothing and necessaries, $264,346.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:

explain the huge increase over last year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The general purpose
of this vote is for the purchase of specialsized clothing, plain clothes for discharged men, badges and miscellaneous articles, and to provide for the clothing of Highland and other regiments which have distinctive uniforms, also articles of clothing and necessaries such as kit bags, brushes, combs, razors, towels, etc. The Estimate is on the probable requirements for the year. The pre-war vote for this item was $700,000. Last year the vote was only $60,000. We utilized to the fullest extent the material which was left over at the end of the war. The greatest difficulty at the present time in regard to clothing and equipment is that we have many of the small sizes and many of the large sizes; but the intermediate sizes are pretty

well out of stock, and as these are the most called for, it is necessary to replace a very large number of the intermediate sizes during the present year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Is the clothing covered

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The cloth is manufactured expressly for this purpose by various mills in the country. Then the contracts for the manufacture of the clothing into suits or for whatever purpose it is used, are let through the Purchasing Commission, formerly known as the War Purchasing Commission.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:

in the ordinary way?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
What about the cost
of the cloth? The textile plants are closed down with no work, and wool is at rock bottom prices, perhaps lower than it has been since eight or ten years before the war. The result is that prices must be exceptionally low on account of the low prices of materials which will enter into the composition of the cloth which will be sold to the department.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION

We have on hand an
abundance of cloth for the present year and, perhaps, for the next year. We will not need to purchase any cloth, but we will need to manufacture that cloth into clothing. I do not know at what price that cloth was bought; I fancy it was secured during the war, and probably at war-time prices.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Is it the policy of the Government to encourage the wearing of kilts and expensive clothing by the regiments?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I do not know that the Government has any policy on the subject. These are matters upon which I, as a member of the Government, am advised by those who are perhaps best able to advise me. We have a very brilliant military staff, who are thoroughly familiar with these things. Where a Highland regiment can be recruited to advantage, and the people of the locality want a Highland regiment, we permit it. The Highland uniform costs considerably more than the ordinary uniform. The Government is not trying to encourage the wearing of one uniform more than another.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: We all know that the Highland regiments are very good, and everybody approves of our raising them, but if a man prefers to go without his trousers and wants to wear a skirt, I do not see why the country should pay for that. The ordinary khaki uniform was used for the great majority of the soldiers in the late war. I have every respect for the Highland regiments, and for both my hon. friends opposite. The Highland regiments did well in the war, but they would possibly have done just as well if they had been wearing trousers, and I do not see why the country should be put to any extra expense in providing Highland uniforms.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION

That is the whole trouble, that; the patriotism of Scotchmen in this country is traded on to keep up the Highland regiments. As long ago as Lord Chatham's time, it was the policy of the British army to enlist a certain number of Highland regiments. Why? Because they fought better. I am not a Highlander, but I could tell you ten thousand tales of heroism that have come about through this principle of encouraging the raising of Highland regiments with all their traditions. The greatest fighter in the world is the Scotch Highlander. I appeal to my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition whether the Mackenzie tartan
should be measured by dollars or cents in the British or Canadian army. If I had the time, I could move this House with what has been accomplished by the Highland regiments. It is a disgrace that in times past the patriotism of men who loved the Highland traditions has been traded upon to bear the extra expense of equipping these men with the Highland uniform.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I had not the slightest intention of disparaging the Highland regiments in any way, or of insinuating that they were not as good as any other regiment. I agree with my gallant friend from Skeena that many thousands of deeds of heroism have been performed by men in the Highland regiments, but my point is that if the commanding officers prefer that their regiments should be clothed in the Highland uniform I do not see why we should be put to the extra expense of equipping them in the Highland uniform.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has been told by the minister that the allowance for Highland regiments is the same as for the line regiments.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I understand the objection that my hon. friend is about to make. The minister told us that he gives the same amount to the Highland regiments as to the others, but he has just told us also that we have had to buy clothing since the war. We have had to get a large amount of new Highland clothing, although we should have had a lot of this, as well as ordinary khaki clothing, left over from our purchases during the war. That is the point I wish to make; I say that there was no necessity for purchasing Highland uniforms, which are very costly, as the minister says.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: We have a lot of Highland clothing on hand, but we have not the particular tartan required by this regiment. maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION

I am a Highlander myself; there is not a drop of any other blood in my veins, and I do not see any valid objection to an Englishman, a Scotchman, or an Irishman joining a Highland regiment if he wishes. He is entitled to do so, and

some of the bravest men under my command were of these nationalities. I do not think that there is any objection, as the hon. member said, to men other than Scotchmen, joining Highland regiments.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: There is no implication.

speechtext: Take it back.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I do not want to misrepresent the hon. gentleman. However, what I want to point out is that the kilt the Highlander wears will outlast at least ten pairs of trousers.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
It is well known in the British Army that the uniform of the Highlander, although it costs more than the uniform of the linesman, gives greater service. I do not wish to make a jest of this matter at all, but I may say that there were men under my command who went to the war with kilts twenty years old, almost as good as new, and they fought in them for a year or two. There is no question that the kilt costs about twice or three times as much as a pair of trousers, but I firmly believe that it will outlast twenty pairs of trousers. I think the Minister of Militia would be acting wisely if he issued kilts to these Highland regiments in lieu of trousers, without making the regiments pay the difference in cost between the kilts and the trousers. The trousers cost something like $5 a pair, while the kilts cost $12, and it means quite a burden for the regiments to pay this difference. Now, there is no question about being able to recruit a Highland regiment if it is properly officered, and as regards their conduct, it is not necessary for me to say anything. We have besides myself one commanding officer here in this House who had charge of a Highland regiment, and he can tell of the actions of the Highlanders as well as I can. No one can doubt that, from the days of Pitt down to the present time, the Highlanders have always been ip the hardest part of the fight, ready to play the part of men, regardless of what nationalities such regiments might have been composed of. I know that many an Irishman has fought nobly in the ranks of the Highlanders, and altogether I do not think that

speechtext:
I do not wish to pursue
the question of the relative merits of kilts over trousers, but I want some information as to what the minister estimates will be the cost of the full uniform for private soldiers.

speechtext:

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: George Etienne Cartier.

speechtext: Well, it is an unpronounceable name. Anyhow, I want to say for the information of that gentleman that, according to the best authority, a Highland regiment was formed after the capture of Palestine, known as the Jordan Highlanders, and they experienced considerable difficulty in deciding upon a motto, but finally devised one. It was: "No advance without security."

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
What
amounts have been expended in previous years on the manufacture of clothing? The minister, perhaps, can give us off-hand the various amounts spent on manufacture alone.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I cannot split the item;
I have the amounts voted. In 1905, it was $430,000; in 1906-7, $317,000, in 1907-8, $331,000; in 1910, $350,000; in 1911, $445,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: What was spent purely on manufacturing the clothing?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I cannot give that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
How many men does the
minister expect to clothe on $220,000?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
We have from 40,000
to 50,000 to clothe this year in addition to those already supplied. We have certain sizes already made.
Mr. POWER. How many will be clothed out of this money?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
The best way to arrive
at that would be to work it out at $7 or $8 apiece.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
That is not satisfactory.
The minister comes with an item of $220,000. How did he arrive at that sum? On what did he base his calculations? I do not want to submit any catch questions, but I want information.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: The figures supplied by the Quarter-Master General, after going over the stores, show that we have uniforms in odd sizes for from ten to fifteen thousand men. There will be, according to him, twenty-five to thirty thousand uniforms to be made new. Now that is as near an estimate as I can give-it may run a little more, it may run a little less.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Has the minister any
idea what number of uniforms were left over after demobilization?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Over 250,000 suits were on hand after the armistice.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: How many have we now on hand?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Of course our stock was badly depleted by giving suits to men who desired them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: In what way?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: To returned men on demobilization.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I would like to know from the minister what nuniber he has in stock?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: We have still in stock about 75,000 suits of odd sizes and ten to twelve thousand suits, perhaps fifteen thousand, will be used this year. We also have in stock cloth for the manufacture of approximately 50,000 new uniforms.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Have any uniforms been disposed of by the Department of Militia, or by the Purchasing Commission, since the armistice, and to whom?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: None since the armistice.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I think the minister answered yesterday that some cloth had been disposed of?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I think the minister stated that some military cloth, or cloth to be used for military purposes, had been disposed to fulfil certain contracts with Roumania?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
No, I did not say that.
I said a street rumour had come to me to that effect. I made particular inquiry of the department to-day in respect to that rumour, and my information is that no cloth and no goods were disposed of by or through the Militia Department to Roumania.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Or by the Purchasing Commission either?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Not to the Purchasing Commission for Roumania either. I said last night, or when the Estimates were up before, that I had heardKa street rumour from a Montreal man that he had procured some military cloth which he had made up for Roumania. On inquiry at the department to-day I find that no goods were sold to Roumania by the Militia Department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
I had occasion, either last year or the year before, to make application on behalf of one of my constituents to the War Purchasing Commission for some military cloth-some khaki cloth-and I was told that they had disposed of large stocks, and that the last stock was about to be disposed of. I know that returned soldiers and civil servants were permitted to buy from the War Purchasing Commission certain military cloth.
I do not wish to imply that this came through the Militia Department, but this was khaki cloth bought for the purposes of the war.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: I think I can give the information now. Before the armistice certain condemned clothing was disposed of through the War Purchasing Commission. Since the armistice none has been disposed of. We cannot tell where the clothing that was sold to the War Purchasing Commission went, and we would have no means of knowing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Then the only military clothing in the possession of the War Purchasing Commission either before or after the armistice was, if I understand the minister, condemned military clothing? Is that statement correct?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext:
No stores that were unused or new or anything of the kind, that came into our hands, were sold or disposed of from the department after the armistice. Prior to the armistice it is just possible

that some of the cancelled orders-because there were a lot cancelled at the time- were sold by the War Purchasing Commission, but they did not go through our department in any way.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: It is now one o'clock. May I suggest to the minister that we pass this item with the understanding that we may later discuss anything relevant to it?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: If the item is passed I have no objection.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CLAIM OF MR. GEORGE B. ALDERSON FOR COMPENSATION
speechtext: Under protest and on division.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
On the motion of Right Hon. Mr. Meighen the House adjourned at 12.55 a.m.
Wednesday, April 20, 1921.
